## Semester Roadmap & Three-Level OB Mental Map

> [!abstract] Why Lecture Order Works Best When Anchored to One Mental Map
> Rather than memorizing dozens of isolated theories, picture every topic in **Lessons 1–14** inside one unified architecture: **Organizational Behaviour is a three-level contingency system (`Behavior = f(Person, Situation)`)**.
>
> 1. **Macro Frame First (Lessons 1–2)**: Learn the three analytical levels (*Individual, Group, Organizational*) and the invisible social control system of *Organizational Culture*.
> 2. **Micro & Meso Core (Lessons 3–9)**: Zoom into how individuals perceive and differ (*Lesson 3*), combine into teams (*Lesson 4*), follow and resist leaders (*Lessons 5–6*), experience emotions, attitudes, and stress (*Lesson 7*), communicate through change (*Lesson 8*), and clash or innovate through diversity (*Lesson 9*).
> 3. **System Design, Motivation & Power (Lessons 10–14)**: Step back up to structural design & HR systems (*Lesson 10*), technological/algorithmic control (*Lesson 11*), motivation & job design (*Lesson 12*), bounded decisions & organizational learning (*Lesson 13*), and conflict, power, politics & negotiation (*Lesson 14*).

![Three-Level OB Contingency System](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460-support/assets/01-ob-three-level-map.svg)
*Figure 0.1: Integrated Three-Level OB Model (`Inputs -> Processes -> Outcomes`) across Individual (Micro), Group/Team (Meso), and Organizational (Macro) levels, paired with Katz skills, Mintzberg roles, and Luthans' empirical breakdown.*

| Manager advancing rapidly via politics/socializing rather than unit performance | **Luthans' Managerial Activities** | **Successful** (`48%` networking) ≠ **Effective** (`44%` communication, `28%` traditional mgmt) | *Mistaking Mintzberg's Figurehead or Katz's Conceptual skill for Luthans' empirical split* | [§1.4](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%231.4%20Managers%27%20Work%3A%20Fayol%2C%20Mintzberg%2C%20Katz%2C%20and%20Luthans) |

| High standards + zero fear of humiliation when admitting an early error or asking for help | **Edmondson Learning Zone** | **High Psych Safety + High Accountability** = Learning; High Standards + Low Safety = **Anxiety Zone** | *Thinking high psychological safety means "Comfort Zone" (niceness without standards)* | [§4.6](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%234.6%20Psychological%20Safety%20%C3%97%20Accountability%20%28Edmondson%2C%201999%29) |
| Skilled, confident veteran engineers need zero micromanagement on a familiar sprint | **Hersey–Blanchard `R4` → Delegating** | **Able & Willing** (`R4`) needs **Low Task + Low Relationship**; **Able & Unwilling/Insecure** (`R3`) needs **Participating** | *Assuming Fiedler lets the leader flex style freely (Fiedler treats LPC style as fixed!)* | [§5.3](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%235.3%20Contingency%20Models%3A%20Fiedler%2C%20Hersey%E2%80%93Blanchard%2C%20and%20Path%E2%80%93Goal) |
| Audience feels **68%** confident they understood a charismatic talk despite scoring only **56%** | **Menges et al. (2015) Awestruck Effect** | **Attention narrows → Self shrinks → Deference rises**; *"feeling informed is enough"* + emotional suppression | *Assuming charismatic leaders welcome upward bad news (considerate ones do; charismatic ones mute emotion!)* | [§6.2](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460%20-%20Organizational%20Behavior%20and%20Leadership%236.2%20Menges%2C%20Kilduff%2C%20Kern%20%26%20Bruch%20%282015%29%3A%20Awe%20and%20the%20Awestruck%20Effect) |

## 1. Lesson 1: Introduction to Organizational Behaviour

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 1 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 1*)
> Lesson 1 establishes what Organizational Behaviour (**OB**) studies, why systematic **evidence-based management (EBM)** outperforms gut intuition, how **contingency variables** govern every OB claim, and what managers actually do (**Fayol, Mintzberg, Katz, Luthans**) alongside modern workforce challenges.

### 1.1 Defining Organizational Behaviour and Its Three Levels
**Organizational Behaviour (OB)** is a field of study that investigates the impact that **individuals**, **groups**, and **structure** have on behavior within organizations, for the purpose of applying such knowledge toward improving an organization's effectiveness. OB matters practically because technical excellence alone rarely saves a failing workplace; most operational breakdowns trace back to **human coordination, leadership, motivation, communication, and culture**.

OB explicitly studies what happens at **three nested levels** (*see Figure 0.1*):
1. **Individual Level (Micro)**: Diversity, personality, values, perception, attitudes, emotions, stress, motivation, and individual decision-making.
2. **Group / Team Level (Meso)**: Group dynamics, team composition, psychological safety, leadership, communication, power, politics, and conflict.
3. **Organizational System Level (Macro)**: Organizational culture, structure and design, algorithmic/technological control, HR systems, and organizational change.

Within this three-level system, **inputs** (antecedents such as personality or structure) flow through **processes** (actions such as decision-making, communication, and motivation) to produce six classic **OB outcomes**:
- **Attitudes & Stress** (satisfaction, well-being, burnout)
- **Task Performance** (core job output quality and quantity)
- **Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB)** (discretionary extra-role helping beyond formal job descriptions — *e.g., mentoring a new hire without overtime pay*)
- **Withdrawal Behavior** (absenteeism, lateness, turnover)
- **Group Cohesion** (shared commitment to stay together and succeed)
- **Organizational Functioning / Productivity** (profitability, innovation, and survival).

### 1.2 Systematic Study, Evidence-Based Management (EBM), and Intuition
Human intuition (*"gut feelings"* about who will perform well or why turnover spiked) often misleads managers because everyday observation suffers from selective memory and cognitive bias. To overcome guesswork, OB pairs two rigorous pillars:
- **Systematic Study**: Looking at relationships, attempting to attribute **causes and effects**, and drawing conclusions based on **scientific evidence** gathered under controlled conditions rather than anecdotes.
- **Evidence-Based Management (EBM)**: Complementing systematic study by basing managerial decisions on the **best available scientific evidence** (*Sample Exam Q1 & Lesson 1*), rather than copying fads or trusting status-quo habits. Intuition works best only as an informed supplement when an expert has accumulated years of valid pattern feedback (*explored deeply in Lesson 13*).

### 1.3 Why Contingency Variables Rule Out Universal "Always" Laws
Unlike physics, human behavior in organizations rarely obeys universal laws (*"money always motivates"* or *"flat structures always beat tall hierarchies"*). Because human beings are complex and respond to social context, OB theories rest on **contingency variables** — situational conditions that moderate the relationship between an independent variable $X$ and a dependent variable $Y$:

$$\text{If } X \text{ occurs} \implies Y \text{ follows, ONLY UNDER CONDITION } Z\text{ (Contingency Variable)}$$

For example, high **work autonomy** raises motivation when employees seek personal growth (**high Growth-Need Strength**), whereas it can generate anxiety if employees lack role clarity or training. Anytime an exam option claims an OB intervention works *"universally in all organizations without exception"*, treat that extreme quantifier as a major **distractor red flag**.

### 1.4 Managers' Work: Fayol, Mintzberg, Katz, and Luthans
OB distinguishes *what organizations call managers* (individuals who achieve goals through other people) by four complementary frameworks tested frequently on BI exams:

1. **Henri Fayol — Four Management Functions** *(see Lesson 8 Q6)*:
   - **Planning**: Defining an organization's goals, establishing an overall strategy, and developing plans to coordinate activities.
   - **Organizing**: Determining what tasks are to be done, who is to do them, how tasks are grouped, who reports to whom, and where decisions are made.
   - **Leading**: Motivating employees, directing others, selecting effective communication channels, and resolving conflicts.
   - **Controlling**: Monitoring performance, comparing actual outcomes against goals, and correcting significant deviations.

2. **Henry Mintzberg — Ten Managerial Roles (Three Categories)**:
   - **Interpersonal Roles**: *Figurehead* (symbolic ceremonies), *Leader* (hiring, training, motivating), *Liaison* (maintaining outside contacts/networks).
   - **Informational Roles**: *Monitor* (collecting internal/external intelligence), *Disseminator* (transmitting info inward), *Spokesperson* (representing the unit outward).
   - **Decisional Roles**: *Entrepreneur* (initiating improvement projects), *Disturbance Handler* (correcting unexpected crises), *Resource Allocator* (assigning budgets/time), *Negotiator* (bargaining with unions, clients, or suppliers).

3. **Robert Katz — Three Essential Management Skills**:
   - **Technical Skills**: Applying specialized knowledge or expertise (*vital at entry-level supervision*).
   - **Human (People) Skills**: Understanding, communicating with, motivating, and supporting others individually and in groups (*see Lesson 8 Q1* — essential at **all** hierarchical levels!).
   - **Conceptual Skills**: Mental ability to analyze and diagnose complex, ambiguous situations (*dominant at top executive levels*).

4. **Fred Luthans — Effective vs. Successful Managers (Empirical Contrast)**:
   Luthans studied **450+ managers** performing four activities: *Traditional Management* (decision-making, planning, controlling), *Communication* (exchanging routine info & paperwork), *Human Resource Management* (motivating, disciplining, training, staffing), and *Networking* (socializing, politicking, interacting with outsiders).

| Manager Profile (Criterion) | Traditional Mgmt | Communication | HRM | Networking | Key Takeaway |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Average Manager** | `32%` | `29%` | `20%` | `19%` | Balanced split across daily tasks |
| **Successful Manager** *(speed of promotion)* | `13%` | `28%` | `11%` | **`48%`** | Socializing & politics drive fast promotions |
| **Effective Manager** *(unit quantity/quality & staff satisfaction)* | `19%` | **`44%`** | `26%` | `11%` | **Communication & people care** drive real performance |

> [!warning] Look-Alike Trap — Effective vs. Successful vs. People Skills
> Do **not** assume the fastest-promoted manager (**Successful** = `48%` Networking) is the highest-performing team builder (**Effective** = `44%` Communication + `26%` HRM). On MCQs linking manager performance and subordinate commitment, look for **Communication / People Skills**, not Networking!

### 1.5 Historical Roots & Contemporary Workplace Challenges
Modern OB builds on the **Hawthorne Studies (Western Electric, 1920s–30s)**, which accidentally revealed that changing lighting did not explain worker output alone — **social norms, group sentiment, and feeling observed/cared for** shaped productivity far more strongly than mechanical incentives (*shifting management from pure Taylorist engineering to human relations*). Today's OB applies that same lens to **globalization & cross-cultural teams**, **AI & algorithmic management** (*Lesson 11*), **remote/gig flexibility**, **ethical dilemmas**, and **psychosocial health**.

> [!question]- Active Recall & Look-Alike Check — Lesson 1
> 1. **Q:** Why can OB *not* promise that "autonomous teams always outperform hierarchies"?
>    **A:** Because OB obeys **contingency variables** ($Z$) such as task routineness, national/organizational culture, and employee growth need.
> 2. **Q:** In Luthans' study, which activity accounts for the largest share of time among **effective** managers vs. **successful** managers?
>    **A:** Effective managers spend **`44%` on Communication** (and `26%` on HRM); successful (fast-promoted) managers spend **`48%` on Networking**.
> 3. **Q:** What distinguishes **OCB** from core **Task Performance**?
>    **A:** Task performance covers formal job duties; **OCB** is discretionary, unrequired helping behavior (*e.g., defending the firm's reputation or helping overloaded peers*) that still boosts unit functioning.
> 4. **Q:** Which Fayol function defines goals and strategy? Which resolves conflicts?
>    **A:** Defining goals = **Planning** (*Lesson 8 Q6*); resolving conflicts & motivating = **Leading**.

## 2. Lesson 2: Organizational Culture

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 2 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 16 & Ch. 5*)
> Lesson 2 explains how culture acts as an invisible **social control system**, how founders and socialization keep it alive, how the **Culture Iceberg** links physical symbols and org charts to hidden assumptions, how national culture (Hofstede/Brooks) interacts with firm identity, and how to diagnose any company using **Groysberg et al.'s (2018) 8 Culture Styles**.

### 2.1 Organizational Culture as Social Control ("How We Do Things Around Here")
**Organizational culture** is a system of **shared meaning** held by members that distinguishes the organization from others. Unlike formal job descriptions or compliance manuals, culture functions as **social control**: members internalize what is rewarded, tolerated, or taboo (*e.g., Pixar's core norms of peer candor, psychological safety in Braintrust reviews, and story-first craft*), regulating behavior automatically even when no supervisor is watching.

Culture matters for three strategic reasons highlighted in Lesson 2:
1. **Drives Behavior & Performance**: It guides daily trade-offs (*speed vs. zero-defect safety; individual heroics vs. helping peers*).
2. **Creates Internal Identity**: Gives employees shared meaning, boundary definition (*who belongs here*), and commitment.
3. **Shapes External Identity**: Signals reputation to customers, regulators, and job applicants (**Person–Organization Fit** — *e.g., PepsiCo's aggressive results focus vs. a luxury hotel's anticipatory caring; Richard Branson's Virgin Group entrepreneurial irreverence*).

### 2.2 Culture Creation, Maintenance, and Socialization
Cultures do not materialize randomly; they are locked in through three interconnected **maintenance mechanisms** (*Robbins & Judge diagram, Slide 16 — tested directly in Lesson 8 Q9!*):

$$\text{Founder's Philosophy} \longrightarrow \begin{cases} \text{1. Selection Criteria (hire P–O fit)} \\ \text{2. Top Management (role modeling \& norms)} \\ \text{3. Socialization (onboarding reality)} \end{cases} \longrightarrow \text{Maintained Organizational Culture}$$

- **Founder's Philosophy**: Founders hire and retain only people who think and feel like they do, and their own behavior sets the blueprint (*e.g., Steve Jobs at Apple; Elon Musk at Tesla*).
- **Selection**: Identifies and hires candidates whose values match the culture (*and lets mismatched applicants self-select out*).
- **Top Management**: Senior executives establish unspoken norms through what they measure, reward, ignore, or punish in crises.
- **Socialization**: Adapts new hires to existing norms across three stages (*R&J Ch. 16*):
  1. **Prearrival**: Expectations and values carried in before day one.
  2. **Encounter**: Reality check on joining, where expectations confront actual workplace norms (*highest shock risk*).
  3. **Metamorphosis**: Work adjustment where the newcomer masters norms, feels accepted, and commits (*reducing early turnover*).

| Culture Strength | Core Advantage | Hidden Liability (Exam Trap!) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Strong Culture** *(core values intensely held & widely shared)* | Reduces need for heavy formal bureaucracy; builds loyalty, predictable alignment, and lower turnover | Creates **institutional inertia**, **groupthink**, resistance to strategic change, and M&A clash (*"culture eats strategy for breakfast"*) |
| **Weak Culture** | Permits local unit flexibility and easy rapid pivots | Weak identity, fragmented coordination, reliance on rigid rules |

### 2.3 The Culture Iceberg, Workspaces, Ceremonies & Tall vs. Flat Hierarchies
A vital diagnostic skill in Lesson 2 (echoing Schein and **Dawson & Andriopoulos, 2021**) is reading **above** and **below** the waterline of the **Culture Iceberg** (*Figure 2.1a*):
- **Surface Manifestations (Above Water — Visible)**: *Physical symbols* (Google campus playfulness vs. Credit Suisse formal marble), landmark headquarters (*Apple Park ring, Empire State Building*), *dress codes*, *ceremonies/rituals* (annual awards, welcome hazing, Town Halls), stories, jargon, and structural charts.
- **Deep Basic Assumptions (Below Water — Invisible Core)**: *Mental schemes*, *unwritten rules* (who can interrupt whom), *actual status dynamics*, *values and norms*, and *shared emotional attitudes*. Changing surface dress codes or buying ping-pong tables **without** changing leadership incentives or assumptions leaves deep culture untouched!

Structural span also shapes daily culture and autonomy (*Lesson 2 comparison for `~4,096` front-line workers*):
- **Tall Structure (`span = 4`, `7` hierarchical levels)**: Requires **`1,365` managers**, creating slower vertical approvals, tighter supervision, and high status distance.
- **Flat Structure (`span = 8`, `5` hierarchical levels)**: Requires only **`585` managers** (fewer than half!), widening autonomy and lowering overhead costs — though managers stretch thinner (*see Lesson 10 §10.1*).

Across *R&J Ch. 16* & Dawson & Andriopoulos, seven descriptive characteristics profile any firm's culture: *Innovation & risk-taking, Attention to detail, Outcome orientation, People orientation, Team orientation, Aggressiveness, and Stability*.

### 2.4 Subcultures, Countercultures, and Professional Cultures
Large organizations rarely hold a single monolithic culture (*Lesson 2 Slide 29 & Lesson 8 Q7*):
- **Dominant Culture**: Expresses the **core values shared by a majority** of the organization's members (*creating macro distinctiveness*).
- **Departmental Subcultures**: Develop inside units (*e.g., R&D vs. Finance vs. Sales*) that retain core dominant values **plus** values unique to their functional problems.
- **Counter-cultures**: Actively **challenge or reject** the dominant corporate values (*often emerging after hostile acquisitions or among alienated tech teams*).
- **Professional Cultures**: Loyalty to occupational standards across firm boundaries (*e.g., surgeons, auditors, software engineers*).

### 2.5 National Culture Frameworks (`Brooks`, `Hofstede`, `High/Low Context`)
Multinationals fail when national norms collide with corporate headquarters culture (*as shown in the **American Factory** Netflix documentary case, Lesson 2 Slide 34: Chinese Fuyao glass-plant militarized top-down obedience & `12-hour` overtime norms clashing with US union autonomy & safety rights*).
- **Brooks (2018) Six Factors Shaping National Culture**: *History, Geography/climate, Political/legal system, Religion/beliefs, Economic development, and Language/demographics*.
- **Hofstede Dimensions (Intro in Lesson 2; full 6 in Lesson 9)**:
  1. **Power Distance (PDI)**: Degree to which less powerful members accept unequal power distribution (*Lesson 2 radial chart: high in Malaysia/China/France vs. low in **Norway/Denmark/Austria** — vital context in Norwegian egalitarian workplaces!*).
  2. **Individualism vs. Collectivism**: Loose ties and personal achievement vs. tight in-group loyalty.
  3. **Uncertainty Avoidance**: Comfort with ambiguity vs. craving strict rules/predictability.
  4. **Masculinity vs. Femininity** *(Assertion/Competition vs. Care/Quality of life)*.
  5. **Long-Term vs. Short-Term Orientation** *(Thrift/persistence vs. quick results/tradition)*.
  6. **Indulgence vs. Restraint** *(added in Lesson 9)*.
- **High-Context vs. Low-Context Communication (`Meyer / Hall`)**: **Low-context** (*USA, Germany, Scandinavia*) conveys meaning **explicitly in direct words**; **High-context** (*Japan, China, Arab world*) embeds meaning in **status, silence, tone, and shared history** (*"reading between the lines"*).

### 2.6 Groysberg et al. (2018): Eight Culture Styles
**Groysberg, Lee, Price & Cheng (HBR, 2018)** mapped organizational cultures along two orthogonal dimensions (*Figure 2.1b*):
- **Horizontal Axis (`People Interactions`)**: **Independence** (autonomy, individual initiative, competition) $\longleftrightarrow$ **Interdependence** (integration, shared coordination, group relationships).
- **Vertical Axis (`Response to Change`)**: **Flexibility** (innovation, openness, diversity, long-term adaptability) $\longleftrightarrow$ **Stability** (consistency, rule adherence, predictability, maintenance).

| Style & Coordinates | Core Emphasis | Benchmark Case | Key Strength | Potential Liability |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Caring** *(Flex + Interdep)* | Warmth, mutual trust, loyalty | **Disney** | High teamwork & engagement | Avoids tough conflict/accountability |
| **2. Purpose** *(Flex + Interdep)* | Idealism, altruism, higher cause | **Whole Foods** | Sustainability & shared mission | May neglect short-term practical efficiency |
| **3. Learning** *(Flex + Indep)* | Exploration, curiosity, creativity | **Tesla** | Innovation & open-mindedness | Risk of chasing unfocused experiments |
| **4. Enjoyment** *(Flex + Indep)* | Fun, excitement, spontaneity | **Zappos** | High morale & joyful creativity | Can lack discipline or structure |
| **5. Results** *(Stab + Indep)* | Achievement, winning, KPIs | **GSK** | Execution focus & merit drive | Short-termism, stress & cutthroat rivalry |
| **6. Authority** *(Stab + Indep)* | Strength, boldness, decisiveness | **Huawei** | Speed & clarity in crises | Politics, fear, suppressed dissent |
| **7. Safety** *(Stab + Interdep)* | Planning, caution, risk prep | **Lloyd's of London** | Preparedness & loss prevention | Stifles innovation & agility |
| **8. Order** *(Stab + Interdep)* | Rules, methodology, respect | **SEC** | Consistency & low chaos | Bureaucratic rigidity & slowness |

### 2.7 Four Culture-Change Levers (& Async Reflection)
As your **async reflection on BI physical study spaces** illustrated, physical environment alone signals cues (*individual focus pods vs. collaborative café tables*), yet lasting **cultural change** requires pulling **four coordinated levers** simultaneously (*Lesson 2 Slide 41*):
1. **Leadership**: Visible executive modeling and crisis behavior (*walking the talk*).
2. **Communication & Behavior**: Articulating new stories, reinforcing desired daily habits, and rewarding dissent/openness.
3. **HR Practices**: Rewriting hiring criteria, onboarding socialization, promotions, and appraisal metrics so people are rewarded for the *new* values.
4. **Symbols**: Reshaping offices, titles, rituals, and ceremonies to anchor the new shared meaning.

> [!question]- Active Recall & Look-Alike Check — Lesson 2
> 1. **Q:** What are the **three primary mechanisms** that maintain an organization's culture after founding? *(Lesson 8 Q9)*
>    **A:** **Selection criteria, top management actions, and socialization** (Prearrival $\to$ Encounter $\to$ Metamorphosis).
> 2. **Q:** Distinguish Groysberg's **Learning** (`Tesla`) vs. **Purpose** (`Whole Foods`) vs. **Results** (`GSK`) culture styles.
>    **A:** *Learning* = Flexibility + Independent (exploration/autonomy); *Purpose* = Flexibility + Interdependent (idealism/altruism); *Results* = Stability + Independent (achievement/KPI winning).
> 3. **Q:** Why can a **strong culture** actually **hurt** a firm undergoing digital transformation?
>    **A:** Intense shared norms act as behavioral blinders and institutional inertia, resisting unfamiliar strategies (**liability against change & M&A integration**).
> 4. **Q:** A factory has 4,096 workers. Roughly how many managers are eliminated by widening span of control from `4` (7 levels) to `8` (5 levels)?
>    **A:** Drops from **`1,365` to `585` managers** — removing `780` managerial positions while shifting toward flatter autonomy.

## 3. Lesson 3: Perception, Personality, and Individual Differences

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 3 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 5 & Ch. 6*)
> Lesson 3 builds the micro foundation of OB: **people react to their *perception* of reality, not objective reality itself**. We trace top-down perceptual filters (*Invisible Gorilla*), **Kelley's Attribution Theory** vs. attribution biases, workplace shortcut errors, the **Pygmalion self-fulfilling prophecy**, and how **Big Five traits, Values, Situation Strength, and Trait Activation** predict workplace behavior.

### 3.1 Perception Mechanics: Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Selective Blindness
**Perception** is the cognitive process by which individuals organize and interpret sensory impressions in order to give meaning to their environment. What makes perception critical in OB is that **behavior tracks *perceived* reality**: two analysts receiving identical feedback react oppositely depending on their filters. Three interacting factors shape perception:
- **Perceiver**: Attitudes, motives, interests, past experience, and expectations.
- **Target**: Novelty, motion, sounds, size, background, and similarity.
- **Situation (Context)**: Time, work setting, and social atmosphere.

To handle sensory overload, human cognition runs two parallel streams:
- **Bottom-Up Processing**: Data-driven construction starting from raw sensory inputs (*seeing a flat tyre*).
- **Top-Down Processing**: Schema-driven interpretation guided by prior knowledge, expectations, and stereotypes (*assuming a quiet colleague is "unambitious"*).

Top-down filtering produces **selective attention**, **inattentional blindness** (*Simons & Chabris' **Invisible Gorilla** experiment*: viewers counting basketball passes fail to notice a gorilla walking straight across center court!), and **change blindness** (*missing big background swaps while focused elsewhere*). **Schemas** (mental templates built from experience) speed up routine decisions, yet silently lock in errors when situations shift.

![Kelley Attribution Cube, Perceptual Biases, and Pygmalion Effect](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460-support/assets/03-kelley-attribution-biases.svg)
*Figure 3.1: (a) Kelley's 3-Cue Attribution Decision Tree (`Distinctiveness`, `Consensus`, `Consistency`); (b) Look-alike attribution biases and perceptual shortcuts; (c) Pygmalion & Golem self-fulfilling prophecy loop.*

### 3.2 Kelley's Attribution Theory and Bias Traps
**Attribution Theory** explains how we judge people differently depending on the meaning we attribute to a behavior — specifically whether an observed action was caused **internally** (*under the person's personal control: low effort, lack of skill*) or **externally** (*forced by the situation: broken software, impossible deadline*).

**Harold Kelley's Covariation Model** evaluates three diagnostic cues (*Figure 3.1a*):

| Cue | Diagnostic Question | Internal Cause Pattern | External Cause Pattern |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Distinctiveness** | Does the person behave this way across **many different tasks** or **only this unique task**? | **LOW** *(fails across all tasks — it's their habit)* | **HIGH** *(fails ONLY here — unusual task)* |
| **2. Consensus** | Do **peers facing the same situation** respond the **same way**? | **LOW** *(only this person failed; peers succeeded)* | **HIGH** *(everybody failed on this same territory)* |
| **3. Consistency** | Does the person respond this way **consistently over time**? | **HIGH** *(happens every quarter)* | **HIGH** *(every time system fails) or* **LOW** *(one-off fluke)* |

> [!warning] Look-Alike Trap — FAE vs. Actor–Observer vs. Self-Serving Bias
> Exam vignettes love swapping who is judging whom! Use this exact rule:
> - **Fundamental Attribution Error (FAE)**: When judging **OTHER people's** behavior, we systematically **underestimate external situational factors** and **overestimate internal personality/ability factors** (*blaming a late teammate's "laziness" instead of metro delays*).
> - **Actor–Observer Effect**: Same event, **two viewpoints**: observers blame **your internal traits**, whereas you (the actor) see **external situational constraints**.
> - **Self-Serving Bias**: Ego protection over **OUR OWN** outcomes — we credit **successes to internal skill/effort**, and blame **failures on external bad luck or unfair grading**.

### 3.3 Shortcuts in Judging Others & The Pygmalion Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
In hurried hiring interviews and annual appraisals, managers rely on five mental shortcuts:
- **Selective Perception**: Picking out fragments that fit our interests/expectations (*accountant spots cost waste; marketer spots branding flaws*).
- **Halo Effect (and Horns Effect)**: Letting **one single positive trait** (*e.g., charm or Ivy League degree*) color the entire evaluation positively — or one negative trait (**Horns Effect**) poison every unrelated rating.
- **Contrast Effect**: Evaluating someone's traits relative to people **just encountered** rather than against an objective standard (*an average candidate after three terrible interviews looks brilliant!*).
- **Projection**: Attributing one's own characteristics/feelings to others.
- **Stereotyping**: Judging someone based on one's perception of the **group** to which they belong.

Crucially, expectations do not remain passive inside the manager's head — they reshape reality through the **Self-Fulfilling Prophecy** (*Merton* / *Rosenthal*, *Figure 3.1c*):
- **Pygmalion Effect**: Manager holds **high expectations** $\to$ gives richer coaching, stretch projects, and warmer feedback $\to$ employee develops higher self-efficacy (**Galatea effect**) and **performs higher**, confirming the prophecy!
- **Golem Effect**: Manager holds **low expectations** $\to$ withdraws support and micromanages trivial tasks $\to$ performance collapses.

### 3.4 Personality Frameworks: Big Five vs. MBTI & Dark Triad
**Personality** is the sum total of ways in which an individual reacts to and interacts with others (*R&J Ch. 5*).
- **Myers–Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI)**: Categorizes people into `16` types across `4` dichotomies (*Extraverted/Introverted, Sensing/Intuitive, Thinking/Feeling, Judging/Perceiving*). **Exam rule**: Popular as a team conversation tool, yet **unrelated to job performance** and **not valid for hiring selection** because it forces people into artificial binary buckets!
- **The Big Five Model (`OCEAN`)**: The scientifically dominant personality framework with proven cross-cultural predictive validity:

| Big Five Trait | Core Meaning | Strongest Workplace / Leadership Prediction (*R&J Ch. 5*) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **O — Openness to Experience** | Creative, curious, artistically sensitive vs. conventional | Predicts **training proficiency, adaptability, creativity & leadership emergence** |
| **C — Conscientiousness** | Responsible, organized, dependable, persistent | **#1 strongest Big Five predictor of overall job performance** across all occupations! |
| **E — Extraversion** | Sociable, assertive, gregarious vs. reserved | **#1 strongest predictor of leadership emergence**; excels in social/sales roles (higher injury risk if reckless) |
| **A — Agreeableness** | Cooperative, warm, trusting vs. cold/antagonistic | Higher customer service, OCB & low deviance; **lower career earnings** (less tough bargaining) |
| **N — Emotional Stability** *(low Neuroticism)* | Calm, self-confident, secure vs. anxious/insecure | Higher **job & life satisfaction**, lower burnout & stress |

*(Note: Core Self-Evaluation [positive view of self-worth & control] and Proactive Personality also boost performance and entrepreneurship, while Dark Triad traits [Machiavellianism, Narcissism, Psychopathy] are unpacked in Lesson 6 §6.5.)*

### 3.5 Values (`Rokeach`), Fit (`P–J` & `P–O`), Situation Strength & Trait Activation
- **Values (`R&J Ch. 5`)**: Basic enduring convictions about preferred conduct or end-states. **Rokeach Value Survey** separates **Terminal Values** (*desirable end-states: freedom, wisdom, family security*) from **Instrumental Values** (*preferable modes of behavior to get there: honesty, ambition, competence*).
- **Person–Job Fit (`Holland's RIASEC`)**: Matches personality/abilities to specific **job demands** $\implies$ predicts **task performance & satisfaction**.
- **Person–Organization Fit (`P–O Fit`)**: Matches employee **values** to the firm's **culture** $\implies$ predicts **organizational commitment & lower turnover** (*far more critical in dynamic team cultures — see Lesson 2 Selection!*).
- **Two Situation Contingencies Governing When Personality Predicts Behavior** (*R&J Ch. 5 pp. 188–190*):
  1. **Situation Strength Theory**: How strongly rules, norms, and cues constrain behavior across **four components**: *Clarity, Consistency, Constraints, and Consequences*. In a **strong situation** (*e.g., strict nuclear safety protocol or military drill*), everyone acts alike regardless of personality; personality predicts behavior best in **weak situations** (*autonomous startup work*).
  2. **Trait Activation Theory (TAT)**: Predicts **which specific situations make a *relevant* trait express itself** (*e.g., an angry customer activates Agreeableness/Neuroticism; an unstructured innovation brief activates Openness; tight deadlines activate Conscientiousness*).

>    **A:** **External** (*territorial/structural barrier in Region West*), not internal laziness!
> 2. **Q:** Why does **Pygmalion** matter when interpreting **Conscientiousness** vs. **MBTI** in HR?
>    **A:** Use **Conscientiousness / Cognitive tests** (*not MBTI*) for selection, because valid selection avoids stereotype/contrast biases while high **Pygmalion** expectations reinforce employee growth once hired.

## 4. Lesson 4: Groups and Teams

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 4 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 9 & Ch. 10*)
> Lesson 4 bridges from individuals into collective work (**Meso OB**). We establish **Social Identity Theory**, contrast **Tuckman's 5-stage model** against **Punctuated Equilibrium**, unpack six core group properties (including **Social Loafing** and **Cohesiveness × Norms**), separate **Groupthink** from **Groupshift**, differentiate **Work Groups** from **Work Teams**, and master **Edmondson's Psychological Safety** (`2×2` matrix).

### 4.1 Groups, Social Identity Theory, and In-Group vs. Out-Group Dynamics
A **group** consists of two or more interacting and interdependent individuals who have come together to achieve particular objectives (**Formal groups** are defined by the org structure; **Informal groups** emerge naturally around friendships or shared interests).
Why do people invest emotionally in groups? **Social Identity Theory** shows that people derive self-esteem and belonging from group memberships (**in-groups**), leading to **in-group favoritism** and viewing outsiders (**out-groups**) stereotypically. Crucially (*tested directly in Lesson 8 Q8!*), **intergroup competition or threat often *increases* internal group cohesiveness** as members rally together against a perceived rival! (*Dark side*: excessive identification feeds **out-group derogation** and exclusionary cliques.)

### 4.2 Group Development: Tuckman vs. Punctuated Equilibrium
Exam questions frequently test *which* developmental model fits a given group:
1. **Tuckman's Five-Stage Model (General / Ongoing Groups)**:
   - **Forming**: Uncertainty over purpose, structure, and leadership; testing acceptable behavior.
   - **Storming**: Intragroup conflict over who controls the group and what tasks belong to whom (*hierarchy crystallizes as Storming resolves*).
   - **Norming**: Close relationships form, cohesiveness rises, and shared expectations (**norms**) solidify.
   - **Performing**: Group structure is fully functional and energy moves directly to executing the task.
   - **Adjourning**: Wrapping up activities and preparing to disband (*temporary committees/task forces*).
2. **Punctuated-Equilibrium Model (`Gersick` — Temporary Groups WITH Deadlines!)**:
   - Contrary to Tuckman's smooth sequence, **temporary deadline groups** (*e.g., an 8-week student consulting project*) follow a punctuated arc:
     - **Phase 1**: First meeting sets behavioral direction, followed by a long period of **inertia** (*low progress, sticking to initial assumptions*).
     - **Midpoint Transition (`exact 50% time mark`)**: Realizing half the time is gone shocks the group into dropping old patterns, adopting new perspectives, and re-anchoring action!
     - **Phase 2**: Second period of sustained execution leading to a final **burst of activity** to finish right at the deadline.

> [!warning] Look-Alike Trap — Tuckman vs. Punctuated Equilibrium
> Never pick Tuckman when the prompt emphasizes a **temporary group with a fixed deadline that shows Phase 1 inertia followed by a dramatic midpoint awakening** — that specific signature belongs 100% to **Punctuated Equilibrium**!

### 4.3 Six Group Properties: Roles, Norms, Status, Size, Cohesiveness & Diversity
1. **Roles**: Expected behavioral patterns tied to a social position. Three sub-concepts matter: *Role Perception* (how you think you should act), *Role Expectations* (how others expect you to act — e.g. **psychological contract**), and **Role Conflict** (meeting one role expectation makes fulfilling another impossible). *Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment* demonstrated how powerfully situational roles override normal personality when clear constraints are absent.
2. **Norms**: Acceptable standards of behavior shared by members (*performance norms, appearance norms, resource allocation*). Classic evidence: **Hawthorne studies** (peer pressure enforced informal output caps *"ratebusters"* vs *"chisellers"*) and **Asch's line-conformity experiment** (~35–37% conformed to blatantly wrong majority answers out of desire to fit in).
3. **Status (`Status Characteristics Theory`)**: Socially defined rank driven by *(a) power over others*, *(b) ability to contribute to group goals*, and *(c) valued personal characteristics*. High-status members resist conformity pressures more easily and dominate discussion — often silencing lower-status experts unless leaders intervene!
4. **Size & Social Loafing**: Larger groups excel at diverse **fact-finding** (*input gathering*), whereas smaller groups (`~5–7`) excel at **fast action** (*execution*). Why do individuals expend **less effort when working collectively than alone**? **Social Loafing** (*Max Ringelmann's 1913 rope-pulling study*: 3 people pulled at only 2.5× individual force; 8 people at <4×!), driven by **diffusion of responsibility** and believing peers are free-riding. *Remedies*: set clear individual accountability, keep teams small, highlight unique member contributions, and select high-conscientiousness/collectivist contributors.
5. **Cohesiveness × Performance Norms `2×2` Interaction**: Cohesiveness is good **only if performance norms are high**!
   - *High Cohesiveness + High Performance Norms* = **High Productivity** (best).
   - *Low Cohesiveness + High Performance Norms* = **Moderate Productivity**.
   - *Low Cohesiveness + Low Performance Norms* = **Low-to-Moderate Productivity**.
   - *High Cohesiveness + Low Performance Norms* = **Low Productivity** (tightly bonded slacking/sabotage!).
6. **Diversity** (*surface vs. deep-level faultlines — unpacked fully in Lesson 9*).

*Figure 4.1: (a) Edmondson's (1999) Psychological Safety × Accountability zones; (b) Work Group vs. Work Team contrast, Tuckman vs. Punctuated Equilibrium, and Groupthink vs. Groupshift.*

### 4.4 Group Decision-Making Traps: Groupthink vs. Groupshift
Groups generate more complete knowledge, diverse views, and higher acceptance of solutions than individuals — yet suffer slower speed, ambiguity of responsibility, and two infamous pathologies (*Figure 4.1b*):
- **Groupthink** *(Irving Janis; *Challenger* disaster; **Lesson 8 Q3**)*: Occurs when pressures for **consensus and unanimity** inside a cohesive group suppress realistic critical appraisal of alternative courses of action. *Symptoms*: illusion of invulnerability, rationalizing away warnings, stereotyping outsiders, **self-censorship** (*junior managers staying silent when bosses sound enthusiastic*), and **mindguards** protecting the leader from dissent. *Remedies*: keep groups under 10, **leader speaks LAST**, assign a rotating **Devil's Advocate**, and hold a *"second-chance"* meeting.
- **Groupshift (Group Polarization)**: The tendency during group discussion for members to exaggerate their **initial leanings**, moving toward a **more extreme position** (*more cautious if initially cautious, OR much riskier if initially risk-tolerant — diffusion of responsibility makes bold risk easier*).
- **Techniques to Fix Face-to-Face Bias**: **Brainstorming** overcomes criticism fear yet still suffers *production blocking* (waiting your turn while forgetting ideas). The **Nominal Group Technique (NGT)** solves both: members **(1) silently write ideas independently**, **(2) present round-robin without criticism**, **(3) clarify**, and **(4) silently rank/vote**, neutralizing status dominance and Groupthink!

### 4.5 Work Groups vs. Work Teams & Team Effectiveness Model (`R&J Ch. 10`)
A recurring exam staple distinguishes a **Work Group** from a true **Work Team**:

| Dimension | Work Group | Work Team |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Goal** | Share information so each member performs within their area | **Collective performance** requiring joint interdependence |
| **Synergy** | **Neutral** (sometimes negative — social loafing) | **Positive** (*whole > sum of individual inputs*) |
| **Accountability** | **Individual** only | **Individual AND mutual** |
| **Skills** | **Random and varied** | **Complementary** |

- **Five Team Types**: *Problem-solving teams* (discuss quality improvements without authority to implement unilaterally), *Self-managed work teams* (10–15 employees planning, scheduling, and reviewing peers), *Cross-functional teams* (same hierarchical level across different departments solving complex tasks), *Virtual teams* (dispersed digital collaboration requiring extra early trust-building), and *Multiteam systems* (*"teams of teams"*).
- **Robbins & Judge Team Effectiveness Model (3 Pillars)**:
  1. **Context**: Adequate resources, clear leadership/structure, climate of **trust**, performance evaluations rewarding *both* individual & team contribution.
  2. **Composition**: Complementary abilities, Big Five (*Conscientiousness + Openness + Agreeableness*), **role allocation**, diversity, **small size (`5–9`)**, member preferences for teamwork.
  3. **Process**: Common purpose, specific goals, **team efficacy**, **accurate shared mental models**, managed task (not relationship!) conflict, **team reflexivity** (reflecting and adjusting strategy), **transactive memory** (knowing *who knows what*), and minimal social loafing.

### 4.6 Psychological Safety × Accountability (`Edmondson, 1999`)
**Psychological Safety** (Amy Edmondson, 1999) is a **shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking** — speaking up with half-baked ideas, admitting errors, asking naive questions, or challenging a boss **without fear of embarrassment, ridicule, or retaliation**. Notice **what it is NOT**: it is **NOT** *"everyone being nice"* or lowering performance bars! As **Google's Project Aristotle** found across 180+ teams, **psychological safety was the #1 predictor of team effectiveness**.

Crossing **Psychological Safety** with **Accountability / Performance Standards** yields four distinct zones (*Figure 4.1a*):
1. **Apathy Zone** *(Low Safety + Low Standards)*: Disengagement, minimum compliance, mutual protection.
2. **Comfort Zone** *(High Safety + Low Standards)*: Warm friendships, polite avoidance of tough feedback, mediocre output.
3. **Anxiety Zone** *(Low Safety + High Standards)*: Fear, **hidden mistakes**, defensive silence, burnout (*classic **Theranos** and NASA **Columbia/Challenger** danger zone!*).
4. **Learning & High-Performance Zone** *(High Safety + High Standards)*: Candid dissent, rapid error detection, continuous learning, and stretch execution!

> [!question]- Active Recall & Look-Alike Check — Lesson 4
> 1. **Q:** Why does **High Psychological Safety + Low Performance Standards** *fail* to deliver high team effectiveness?
>    **A:** That puts the team in Edmondson's **Comfort Zone** (nice and conflict-free, yet complacent); true learning requires **High Safety + High Accountability**.
> 2. **Q:** In an official course MCQ (*Lesson 8 Q3*), junior managers withhold doubts about an expansion because senior executives are enthusiastic. Groupthink or Groupshift?
>    **A:** **Groupthink** (*self-censorship driven by conformity pressure to agree with leadership*).
> 3. **Q:** What single numerical difference separates a **Work Group** from a **Work Team** on synergy and accountability?
>    **A:** Work Group = **Neutral/negative synergy + Individual accountability**; Work Team = **Positive synergy + Individual & Mutual accountability**.
> 4. **Q:** How does the **Nominal Group Technique (NGT)** outperform standard interacting meetings and brainstorming?
>    **A:** **Silent independent writing** + **round-robin listing** + **silent voting** prevents dominant loud voices from anchoring the room and eliminates production blocking.

## 5. Lesson 5: Leadership Part 1 — Theories and Styles

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 5 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 12*)
> Lesson 5 traces leadership research chronologically: **Traits** (who emerges?) $\to$ **Behaviors** (what do leaders do?) $\to$ **Contingency Fit** (**Fiedler's fixed LPC**, **Hersey–Blanchard `R1–R4`**, **House Path–Goal**) $\to$ **Dyadic & Value-Based Leadership** (**LMX**, **Full-Range Transformational–Transactional**, **Authentic, Ethical, Servant**, and **Substitutes**).

### 5.1 Leadership vs. Management & Emergent vs. Assigned Leadership
**Leadership** is the ability to **influence a group toward the achievement of a vision or set of goals**. While managers rely on **formal positional authority** to bring order, consistency, budgets, and plans (**Management**), **Leadership** copes with change by setting direction, aligning people, and inspiring commitment. Organizations need **both**! Moreover, **assigned** leaders hold formal titles (*VP*), whereas **emergent** leaders earn informal influence from peers (*often driven by competence, vocal participation, and extraversion — Lesson 5 in-slide reflection*).

### 5.2 Trait Theories vs. Behavioral Theories (`Ohio State` & `Michigan`)
- **Trait Theories (Big Five & EI)**: Early searches for a universal "born leader" failed because traits alone ignore followers and context. Modern Big Five meta-analyses prove traits predict **leadership *emergence*** much better than **leadership *effectiveness***:
  - **Extraversion** = strongest trait predictor of **emergence** (high energy/assertiveness).
  - **Conscientiousness** & **Openness to Experience** = link strongly to leader effectiveness.
  - **Emotional Intelligence (EI)** *(empathy & self-regulation)* supports social influence and authentic rapport.
- **Behavioral Theories** shifted focus from *who leaders are* to *what trainable actions leaders do*:
  - **Ohio State Studies**: Found two independent dimensions — **Initiating Structure** (*defining roles, organizing tasks, deadlines*) and **Consideration** (*mutual trust, respect for ideas, warmth*). Both matter: Initiating Structure drives task productivity; Consideration drives follower satisfaction, motivation, and leader ratings!
  - **University of Michigan Studies**: **Production-oriented** (technical/task aspects) vs. **Employee-oriented** (interpersonal relationships & individual needs — strongly linked to higher group productivity and satisfaction).

![Contingency Leadership, Awestruck Charisma, and Destructive Leadership](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460-support/assets/05-leadership-decision-framework.svg)
*Figure 5.1: Integrated Leadership Map — (a) Fiedler LPC vs. Hersey–Blanchard SLT; (b) Full-Range Leadership & Menges et al. Awestruck Effect; (c) Einarsen et al. Destructive Leadership `2×2`; (d) Toxic Triangle & Kelley Followership.*

### 5.3 Contingency Models: Fiedler, Hersey–Blanchard, and Path–Goal
Behavioral models struggled because identical leader behaviors thrived in one crisis and flopped in another. Three **contingency theories** explain *when* task vs. relationship focus works best:

1. **Fiedler's Contingency Model (FIXED Leadership Style!)**:
   - Measures leadership style via the **Least Preferred Coworker (`LPC`) questionnaire**: describing the hardest peer you ever worked with in relatively positive terms = **Relationship-oriented (`High LPC`)**; harsh negative terms = **Task-oriented (`Low LPC`)**.
   - **Critical Exam Rule**: Fiedler assumes a leader's **`LPC` style is FIXED**! Therefore, rather than telling leaders to adapt personalities, Fiedler says either **(a) replace the leader to fit the situation** or **(b) change the situation** across three **situational control** dimensions (ordered by weight):
     1. **Leader–Member Relations**: Confidence, trust, and respect followers feel (*most important!*).
     2. **Task Structure**: Degree to which job assignments are procedurized/clear.
     3. **Position Power**: Formal authority to hire, fire, discipline, and reward.
   - **Fiedler Fit Law**: **Task-oriented (`Low LPC`)** leaders perform best at **both extremes** — **very high control** (*favorable*) AND **very low control** (*unfavorable crisis*); **Relationship-oriented (`High LPC`)** leaders perform best in **moderate control** situations!

2. **Hersey & Blanchard's Situational Leadership Theory (`SLT` — ADAPTABLE Style!)**:
   - Unlike Fiedler, **SLT assumes leaders CAN adapt** across four styles based on **Follower Readiness** (*Ability × Willingness/Confidence*):
     - **`R1` (`Unable & Unwilling / Insecure`)** $\implies$ **Telling / Directing** (*High Task, Low Relationship*: clear, specific instructions).
     - **`R2` (`Unable but Willing / Confident`)** $\implies$ **Selling / Coaching** (*High Task, High Relationship*: explain decisions and train).
     - **`R3` (`Able but Unwilling / Insecure`)** $\implies$ **Participating / Supporting** (*Low Task, High Relationship*: share ideas, encourage voice).
     - **`R4` (`Able & Willing / Confident`)** $\implies$ **Delegating** (*Low Task, Low Relationship*: turn over responsibility!).

3. **House's Path–Goal Theory**:
   - Leaders motivate by clarifying paths to goals and removing roadblocks, flexing across four behaviors: **Directive** (*ambiguous/unstructured tasks*), **Supportive** (*stressful, boring, structured tasks — compensates!*), **Participative** (*ambiguous tasks with expert/internal-locus subordinates*), and **Achievement-Oriented** (*challenging goals for confident teams*).

> [!warning] Look-Alike Trap — Fiedler vs. Hersey–Blanchard (`SLT`)
> - **Fiedler**: Style (`LPC`) is **fixed** $\to$ match/change **situational control** (`Relations`, `Structure`, `Power`).
> - **Hersey–Blanchard SLT**: Leader **adapts style** (`Telling, Selling, Participating, Delegating`) to match **follower ability & willingness (`R1–R4`)**.

### 5.4 Leader–Member Exchange (`LMX`) Theory
Due to limited time and **Conservation of Resources** (*R&J Ch. 18*), leaders do **not** treat every subordinate identically. Early interactions split subordinates into two tiers:
- **In-Group**: High trust, disproportionate attention, mentoring, stretch assignments, and special privileges $\implies$ higher performance, OCB, and satisfaction, lower turnover.
- **Out-Group**: Strictly formal contractual exchanges (`9-to-5` compliance) $\implies$ lower trust and higher alienation.
*Dark side*: If in-group selection relies on demographic similarity rather than merit, **LMX differentiation** breeds perceived organizational injustice and resentment!

### 5.5 Full-Range Leadership Model (`Laissez-Faire`, `Transactional`, `Transformational`)
Bass & Avolio arranged leadership behaviors along an **Effectiveness × Activity** continuum (*Figure 5.1b*):
1. **Laissez-Faire** (*Passive / Ineffective*): Abdicates responsibility and avoids making decisions (*debated in Lesson 6 as passive destructive!*).
2. **Transactional Leadership** *(Motivation via exchange & compliance)*:
   - **Management by Exception — Passive (`MBE-P`)**: Intervenes only after standards fail.
   - **Management by Exception — Active (`MBE-A`)**: Actively monitors errors/deviations to correct them.
   - **Contingent Reward**: Contracts exchange of effort/performance for clear rewards (*strongest transactional builder — actually boosts followers' baseline trust!*).
3. **Transformational Leadership** *(Inspires followers to transcend self-interest for a collective mission — the **4 I's**)*:
   - **Idealized Influence**: Models high ethics, vision, pride, trust, and personal integrity.
   - **Inspirational Motivation**: Communicates high expectations with vivid symbols and compelling vision.
   - **Intellectual Stimulation**: Encourages questioning old assumptions, rational creativity, and problem reframing.
   - **Individualized Consideration**: Coaches each follower personally, listens empathetically, and treats people as unique individuals (*vital contrast with pure Charisma in Lesson 6!*).

**Augmentation Effect**: Transformational leadership builds **on top of** effective Transactional management (*not in place of it!*); pure vision with zero follow-through fails operationally.

### 5.6 Positive Ethics-Anchored Styles & Substitutes for Leadership
- **Authentic Leadership**: Leaders know who they are, what they believe, and act transparently on moral values — building deep trust (*critique: self-reported "authenticity" can excuse blunt egoism unless grounded in ethics*).
- **Servant Leadership**: Goes beyond self-interest to prioritize followers' growth, autonomy, and wellbeing, creating OCB and ethical climate (*stronger fit in non-cutthroat/feminine cultures*).
- **Ethical Leadership**: Both a **moral person** (honest, fair) and a **moral manager** (explicitly rewards ethical conduct & punishes misconduct).
- **Substitutes & Neutralizers (`Kerr & Jermier`, Sample Exam Q9/Lesson 5)**: Certain individual, task, and organizational conditions reduce the need for leadership — **Substitutes** (*high employee expertise, clear routine SOPs, cohesive self-managed teams*) **replace** leader direction positively, whereas **Neutralizers** (*rigid spatial distance, zero reward control*) **block** a leader's ability to influence at all!

## 6. Lesson 6: Leadership Part 2 — Charisma, Followership, and the Dark Side

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 6 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 12 + Menges et al. 2015, Einarsen et al. 2007, Padilla et al. 2007*)
> Lesson 6 flips the bright hero narrative of leadership to ask: **When does charisma blind followers, how do followers themselves co-produce leadership, and how do Dark Triad and destructive leaders ruin organizations?**

### 6.1 Charismatic Leadership (`Weber` & `Robbins & Judge`)
The word *charisma* originates from the Greek word for *"gift."* Sociologist **Max Weber** contrasted three pure sources of legitimate authority:
1. **Traditional Authority**: Derived from custom, inheritance, or sacred continuity (*e.g., monarchy*).
2. **Legal–Rational Authority**: Derived from formal rules, offices, and enacted law (*e.g., bureaucracy*).
3. **Charismatic Authority**: Derived from devotion to an individual leader's perceived **extraordinary heroism, sanctity, or exemplary character**.

In **Robbins & Judge (`Ch. 12`)** and Robert House's attribution theory, **Charismatic Leadership** occurs when followers make attributions of heroic or extraordinary abilities when observing **four key leader behaviors**:
1. **Vision and Articulation**: Holds an idealized future goal clearly superior to the status quo and communicates it in understandable terms.
2. **Personal Risk**: Willing to incur high personal cost, self-sacrifice, and risk to achieve the vision.
3. **Sensitivity to Follower Needs**: Perceptive of others' abilities and responsive to their needs and feelings.
4. **Unconventional Behavior**: Engages in novel, norm-breaking actions that signal courage and competence.

*Are charismatic leaders born or made?* Lesson 6 answers **both**: **Genetics/Personality** tilts individuals (*Extraversion, Emotional Stability, high self-monitoring*), while **behavioral training** (*practicing optimistic framing, vivid metaphors, voice inflection, and dynamic body posture*) measurably increases perceived charisma!

### 6.2 Menges, Kilduff, Kern & Bruch (2015): Awe and the Awestruck Effect
Why can charismatic speeches mesmerize smart people into trusting weak logic or hiding bad news? **Menges et al. (2015)** identified the **Awestruck Effect**: charismatic displays induce the powerful emotion of **awe**, triggering a three-step psychological cascade:

$$\text{Charismatic Display} \longrightarrow \text{1. Attention Narrows} \longrightarrow \text{2. The Self Shrinks} \longrightarrow \text{3. Deference Rises}$$

Charismatic leaders trigger awe via **four signature tactics** (*applied directly to Elizabeth Holmes in Theranos*):
1. **Rhetorical Tactics** (metaphors, contrasts, three-part lists, moral conviction).
2. **Exceptional Performance** (prodigy origin stories — *"dropped out of Stanford at 19"*).
3. **Problem Reframing** (turning routine diagnostics into a crusade — *"saving loved ones from saying goodbye too soon"*).
4. **Self-Sacrifice** (turtlenecks, zero vacations, sleeping at the lab).

Crucially, Menges et al. uncovered **four counter-intuitive empirical traps** often tested on OB exams (*Lesson 6 Slides 20–26*):
- **The Illusion of Learning (`TEDx UHasselt Experiment`)**: After a charismatic talk, listeners **felt `68%` confident** they understood/retained the content while scoring only **`56%` actual recall** — whereas listeners to a *normal* lecture felt **`55%` confident** yet scored **`60%` actual recall**! **Rule**: *"Feeling informed is enough"* under awe, numbing critical scrutiny.
- **Charisma Does Not Need Positive Emotion**: Charismatic leaders frequently weaponize **fear, anger, and out-group hatred** (*see Lesson 6 US polarization data: `72%` Republicans / `63%` Democrats viewing the opposing party as immoral*) to trigger awe-based deference.
- **`2×` Cheating & Unethical Compliance**: Experimental participants exposed to charismatic vs. control leadership were **twice as likely (`2×`) to lie and cheat** for monetary bonus incentives!
- **The Emotional Suppression Paradox (*Charisma vs. Individualized Consideration*)**: *Charismatic leadership* produces **"hearts stirred, faces blank"** — followers suppress their own emotional expression out of deference and fear of spoiling the mood. By contrast, **Individualized Consideration** puts leaders in *listening mode*, increasing follower emotional openness and honest upward warning! (**Golden Quote**: *"If you inspire your team in the morning, you may not hear the bad news in the afternoon."*)

### 6.3 The Dark Side in Practice: Theranos (`Elizabeth Holmes`), `FTX`, and `Charisma on Fire`
Why didn't charisma alone explain **Theranos (`2003–2026`, `\$9bn` peak valuation, `4` fraud counts, `123` months sentence, `\$452m` restitution)** or **FTX**? Because outward charismatic tactics hid a **tyrannical interior**: siloed engineering teams forbidden to talk across units, aggressive NDAs and private-investigator intimidation, and framing **any scientific dissent as personal disloyalty**!
**Klein & House (1995) — *"Charisma on Fire"*** explains why charismatic disasters only ignite when three elements meet:
1. **Spark (Charismatic Leader)**: High vision, risk appetite, and rhetorical skill.
2. **Fuel (Susceptible Followers)**: Low self-clarity, unmet psychological needs, wish to belong.
3. **Oxygen (Conducive Setting)**: Uncertainty, crisis, media hype, and weak governance checks.

### 6.4 Followership: `Blom & Alvesson` and `Kelley (1988/1992)`
Leadership is co-produced by **followers** (*not passively done to them*):
- **Blom & Alvesson — *Leadership On Demand*** *(two R&D units study)*: Followers actively **initiate** leadership when seeking validation or ambiguity relief, and **inhibit** leadership by ignoring managers when autonomous experts don't need them.
- **Robert Kelley (`1988/1992`) Followership Styles** cross two behavioral dimensions (*Independent Critical Thinking* vs. *Dependent Uncritical Thinking* $\times$ *Active* vs. *Passive Engagement*):

| Kelley Style | Thinking Dimension | Engagement | Organizational Role & Dark-Side Risk |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Exemplary (Effective)** | Independent, critical | Active | Challenges flawed plans constructively; defends ethics |
| **Alienated** | Independent, critical | Passive | Cynical veteran who spots flaws yet refuses to step in |
| **Conformist ("Yes-People")** | Dependent, uncritical | Active | Energetic implementers who **enable destructive leaders & Groupthink**! |
| **Passive ("Sheep")** | Dependent, uncritical | Passive | Relies entirely on boss's direction and waits passively |
| **Pragmatist (Survivor)** | Moderate | Moderate | Hedges bets, plays it safe until direction becomes clear |

### 6.5 Destructive Leadership (`Einarsen`), Dark Triad & The Toxic Triangle
**Einarsen, Aasland & Skogstad (2007)** defined **destructive leadership** as systematic and repeated behavior by a leader that violates the legitimate interest of the organization by undermining/sabotaging its goals **and/or** the motivation, well-being, or job satisfaction of subordinates (*Figure 5.1c*). Three active destructive quadrants emerge (*plus Constructive `[+Org / +Sub]`*):
1. **Tyrannical Leadership (`+ Organization / - Subordinates`)**: Pro-corporate quotas and goals, yet achieves them by bullying, intimidating, humiliating, and overworking subordinates (*e.g., aggressive micro-tyrants whose units hit short-term revenue targets*).
2. **Derailed Leadership (`- Organization / - Subordinates`)**: Anti-subordinate **and** anti-organization (*bullying, fraud, embezzlement, sabotage, absenteeism — maximum dual destruction*).
3. **Supportive–Disloyal Leadership (`- Organization / + Subordinates`)**: Pro-subordinate at the **organization's expense** (*allowing chronic slacking, granting unauthorized perks/overtime, hoarding org resources to buy team popularity*).

**The Laissez-Faire Debate (`Lesson 6 Slides 44–46`)**: Is passive, absent *laissez-faire* leadership "destructive"?
- **Skogstad et al. (2007) — YES**: Chronic abdication violates legitimate organizational goals and triggers **role conflict, role ambiguity, and workplace bullying** among peers.
- **Krasikova, Green & LeBreton (2013) — NO (Distinguish Commission vs. Omission)**: Reserve *destructive leadership* for harmful **volitional choices / sins of commission** (*Tyrannical, Derailed, Supportive-Disloyal*); label *Laissez-Faire* and *Incompetent* leadership **sins of omission** (*ineffective absence rather than active destruction*).

Related dark constructs highlighted in Lesson 6:
- **Abusive Supervision**: Sustained display of **hostile verbal and nonverbal behaviors (excluding physical contact)** costing US firms `\$23.8bn/yr`. Driven by interpersonal injustice, negative affect, and family aggression history, it locks into a **retaliation spiral** (*hostile boss $\to$ subordinate CWB/deviance $\to$ harsher retaliation*).
- **The Dark Triad (Three Malevolent Personality Traits)**:
  - **Machiavellianism**: Pragmatic, emotionally detached, manipulative; *"the ends justify the means"*.
  - **Narcissism**: Grandiose self-importance, entitlement, fragile ego needing admiration (*associated with **`+29%` CEO odds** in a `172` Italian CEO study; `~18%` of senior leaders scoring `>4/7` vs `~1%` clinical rate*).
  - **Psychopathy**: Lack of empathy, shallow affect, zero remorse, thrill-seeking impulsivity (*Babiak & Hare **Snakes in Suits**: **`21%`** in a corporate `n=261` executive sample showed elevated psychopathic traits vs. `~1%` general population!*).
- **Normal Personality Extremes vs. Dark Triad**: Fix exaggerated normal traits (*e.g., bluntness*) with **coaching/development**; fix **Dark Triad** risks via **selection/screening**, because coaching often just sharpens manipulators' tactics!
- **The Toxic Triangle (`Padilla, Hogan & Kaiser, 2007`, *Figure 5.1d*)**: Destructive outcomes never stem from one villain alone; they require the interaction of **(1) Destructive Leaders**, **(2) Susceptible Followers** (*Conformers* out of fear/low self-concept + *Colluders* chasing personal gain), and **(3) Conducive Environments** (*instability, perceived threat, cultural values valuing blind authority, absent checks & balances*).

>    **A:** **Awe narrows attention, shrinks the self, and raises deference**, causing followers to **suppress emotional expressions** ("hearts stirred, faces blank") and rely on *"feeling informed"* (`68%` vs `56%` actual recall), unlike **Individualized Consideration**, which invites honest voice.

>    **A:** **Destructive Leaders** + **Susceptible Followers (`Conformers & Colluders`)** + **Conducive Environments** (`instability, threat, weak governance`).

## 7. Lesson 7: Work Environment, Attitudes, Emotions, and Stress

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 7 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 3, Ch. 4 & Ch. 18*)
> Lesson 7 connects **how people feel** (*Job Attitudes, Cognitive Dissonance, EVLN, Emotional Labor*) with **psychosocial work health** (*Stressors vs. Strain, Challenge vs. Hindrance Stressors, JDCS, COR, Effort–Reward Imbalance, JD-R, Burnout, and Norwegian Work Environment law*). Notice in `R&J 19e`, Health & Stress is **Chapter 18**.

### 7.1 Job Attitudes (`ABC Model`), Moderators, and Major OB Attitudes (`R&J Ch. 3`)
**Attitudes** are evaluative statements — favorable or unfavorable — concerning objects, people, or events (*"I hate this schedule"*). Every attitude contains three **ABC components**:
1. **Affective**: The emotional or feeling segment (*"I feel angry about unfair pay"*).
2. **Behavioral**: Intention to act in a certain way (*"I am updating my CV to look for another job"*).
3. **Cognitive**: Description or belief about the way things are (*"My pay is below market peers"*).

Does attitude predict behavior? Only strongly when **moderated** by five factors (*R&J Ch. 3 p. 117*): *attitude importance*, *correspondence to the specific behavior*, *accessibility (frequent expression)*, *absence of overwhelming social pressures*, and *direct personal experience*.

Know all **five major OB job attitudes** cleanly so you never confuse them on an MCQ:
- **Job Satisfaction**: Positive feeling about a job resulting from evaluating its characteristics (*pay, supervision, coworkers, autonomy — strongly boosts OCB, life satisfaction & customer satisfaction; lowers turnover/absenteeism*).
- **Job Involvement**: Degree to which a person identifies psychologically with their job and views perceived performance level as important to self-worth.
- **Psychological Empowerment**: Employees' belief in the degree to which they influence their work environment, competence, meaningfulness of the job, and autonomy.
- **Organizational Commitment**: Identification with a particular organization and its goals — **three sub-components**:
  - **Affective Commitment**: Emotional attachment and belief in org values (*"I stay because I WANT to"* — strongest positive outcomes!).
  - **Continuance Commitment**: Perceived economic/pension/switching cost of leaving (*"I stay because I NEED to / can't afford to quit"*).
  - **Normative Commitment**: Moral obligation to stay (*"I stay because I OUGHT to"*).
- **Perceived Organizational Support (`POS`)** & **Employee Engagement**: **POS** = degree to which employees believe the org values their contributions and cares about their well-being; **Employee Engagement** = intense involvement, satisfaction, and enthusiasm for the work itself.

### 7.2 Cognitive Dissonance & Responses to Dissatisfaction (`EVLN`, *R&J Ch. 3 p. 130*)
- **Cognitive Dissonance (`Leon Festinger`)**: Any incompatibility between two or more attitudes, or between **behavior and attitudes** (*e.g., warning customers about sustainability while working for a heavy polluter*). People seek to reduce discomfort either by altering attitudes, altering behavior, or **rationalizing** the discrepancy — moderated by *(1) importance of the elements*, *(2) degree of perceived personal control/influence*, and *(3) rewards involved*.
- **The `EVLN` Framework** maps **four responses to job dissatisfaction** along two axes (`Constructive–Destructive` $\times$ `Active–Passive`):

| Response | Axes | Behavioral Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Exit** | **Active + Destructive** | Resigning, requesting transfer, actively job hunting |
| **Voice** | **Active + Constructive** | Suggesting workflow fixes, discussing problems with boss, union bargaining |
| **Loyalty** | **Passive + Constructive** | Optimistically waiting for conditions to improve; defending firm publicly |
| **Neglect** | **Passive + Destructive** | Chronic lateness/absenteeism, reduced effort, higher error rates (*quiet withdrawal*) |

### 7.3 Emotions, Moods, Affective Events Theory (`AET`), and Emotional Labor (`R&J Ch. 4`)
Emotions and moods shape everything from interview ratings to decision risk:
- **Emotions vs. Moods**: **Emotions** are intense, discrete reactions directed at a specific object/event and short-lived (*anger at a rude email*); **Moods** are milder, generalized, longer-lasting background states often lacking an obvious trigger (*positive vs. negative affect*).
- **Affective Events Theory (`AET`, *R&J Ch. 4 & Lesson 13*)**: Workplace hassles and uplifts (**Work Events**) trigger real-time **emotional reactions**, which directly drive spontaneous **affect-driven behavior** (*snapping at a peer, helping spontaneously*) and cumulatively shape **job satisfaction & judgment-driven behavior** (*quitting months later*).
- **Emotional Labor (`R&J Ch. 4 pp. 151–153`)**: An employee's expression of organizationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions (*flight attendants cheerful, nurses calm, bill collectors stern*). When **felt emotions** clash with **displayed emotions**, employees experience exhausting **emotional dissonance**, managed in two distinct ways:
  - **Surface Acting**: Hiding true inner feelings and faking required outward expressions (*"put on a fake smile"*). **Exam rule**: Deals with *displayed* emotions $\to$ **exhausting, predicts burnout, low satisfaction, insomnia, and work–family conflict**!
  - **Deep Acting**: Trying to actually **modify true inner feelings** (*reappraising an angry caller as overwhelmed/scared*) to match display rules. Deals with *felt* emotions $\to$ **higher job satisfaction, better performance, better tips/customer rapport**!

### 7.4 Stressors, `JDCS`, `COR`, Effort–Reward Imbalance & `JD-R` (`Lesson 7` + `R&J Ch. 18`)
Notice the clean conceptual chain in **Robbins & Judge Ch. 18**:
$$\text{Potential Stressors} \text{ (Env / Org / Personal)} \longrightarrow \text{Experienced Stress} \text{ (Appraisal + Resources)} \longrightarrow \text{Strain} \text{ (Physiological, Psychological, Behavioral)}$$

1. **Challenge Stressors vs. Hindrance Stressors (Exam Classic!)**:
   - **Challenge Stressors**: Demands associated with workload, tight deadlines, time urgency, and high responsibility $\to$ trigger pressure, yet **often enhance motivation, learning, and performance** (especially with adequate support!).
   - **Hindrance Stressors**: Obstacles blocking goal attainment — **role ambiguity, role conflict, red tape, organizational politics, job insecurity** $\to$ **uniformly negative** effects on strain, performance, and turnover!

2. **Four Stress & Work-Environment Models (`R&J Ch. 18` & `Lesson 7`)**:
   - **Karasek's Job Demand–Control–Support (`JDCS`) Model**: High **job demands** cause dangerous strain mainly when paired with **low job control (autonomy)** and **low social support** (*"High-Strain Job"*). **High Demands + High Control + High Support** = *"Active Learning Job"*!
   - **Job Demands–Resources (`JD-R`, `Bakker & Demerouti`, *R&J p. 642*)**: Most influential modern framework linking two dual processes:
     - **Health-Impairment Pathway**: Chronic excessive **Job Demands** (physical/emotional/hindrance load) deplete energy $\to$ **Burnout / Strain**.
     - **Motivational Pathway**: Abundant **Job Resources** (autonomy, feedback, leader support, growth opportunities) buffer demands AND independently drive **Work Engagement**!
   - **Conservation of Resources (`COR`, `Hobfoll`, *R&J pp. 639–640*)**: People strive to obtain, retain, and protect valued resources (*energy, status, time, autonomy*). **Resource loss hurts disproportionately more than equivalent resource gain helps**, driving defensive withdrawal (*reduced voice, cautious hoarding, LMX differentiation by tired leaders*).
   - **Effort–Reward Imbalance (`ERI`)**: Strain erupts when high sustained effort is met with low financial, esteem, or career **rewards** (*unfair reciprocity*).

3. **Burnout, Workaholism & Psychosocial Risk Context**:
   - **Burnout (`Maslach`)** comprises **three distinct dimensions**: *(1) Emotional Exhaustion* (drained), *(2) Cynicism / Depersonalization* (detaching coldly from clients/work), and *(3) Reduced Personal Efficacy* (feeling ineffective).
   - **Workaholism** *(compulsive internal drive to overwork even off-hours, distinct from healthy engagement)* damages sleep and recovery.
   - **Norwegian Working Environment Context (`Lesson 7`)**: Norwegian labor norms (**Arbeidsmiljøloven / AML**) explicitly treat **psychosocial work environment** (*role clarity, reasonable workload, freedom from bullying/harassment, employee co-determination*) alongside physical safety as employer legal duties. Managing stress combines **individual approaches** (*time management, physical exercise, relaxation, cognitive reframing, social support*) with **organizational approaches** (*goal setting, job redesign/enrichment, realistic selection/placement, employee involvement, wellness & sabbaticals*).

>    **A:** **Surface acting** leaves raw negative felt emotions intact, creating chronic **emotional dissonance**, whereas **deep acting** cognitively modifies felt emotion into alignment.
> 2. **Q:** Classify each response in `EVLN`: *(a) Suggesting a new scheduling roster to your boss*; *(b) Showing up 20 minutes late daily while scrolling social media*; *(c) Quietly trusting leadership to fix budget cuts*.
