## 8. Lesson 8: Communication and Organizational Change

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 8 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 11 & Ch. 16*)
> Lesson 8 examines **why over 90% of a manager's workday is spent communicating** yet misunderstandings dominate, integrating **Watzlawick**, **Hall's Proxemics**, **Allen's Distance Curve**, **Active vs. Reflective Listening**, and the **Channel Richness Matrix** with **Change Management** (*Kotter's change consistency rule, Exhibit 16-8 Resistance Sources, Cooptation vs. Participation, Lewin's 3-Step, Kotter's 8-Step, Action Research, and Appreciative Inquiry*). Note Lesson 8 slides also house **9 Official Course MCQs (`L8.1–L8.9`)** covered in `[Practice](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460-support/Practice)`.

### 8.1 The Communication Process, Perceptual Filters & Watzlawick's Axiom
Rooted in Latin *cum + munia* (*"sharing duties/tasks in common"*), organizational communication transfers **understanding**, not merely data (*AC Milan tactical coordination example, Lesson 8*). In the **Communication Process Model**:
$$\text{Context} \to \text{Sender (Thoughts)} \xrightarrow{\text{Encoding}} \text{Message / Channel} \xrightarrow{\text{Noise \& Perceptual Filters}} \text{Decoding} \to \text{Receiver} \xrightarrow{\text{Feedback Loop}} \text{Sender}$$

Notice what breaks down in practice: *what you think $\neq$ what you intend to send $\neq$ what the receiver decodes* because **perceptual filters** (*culture, status fears, emotions, schemas*) distort both encoding and decoding!
- **Paul Watzlawick (`1967`) First Axiom**: ***"You cannot not communicate."*** Every silence, ignored Slack ping, crossed arm, or delayed reply sends a social message interpreted by receivers (*"Silence = disapproval/disinterest"*).

### 8.2 Non-Verbal Communication, Proxemics (`Hall`), and the `Allen (2007)` Distance Curve
When verbal words contradict body language or vocal tone, **receivers overwhelmingly believe the non-verbal channel** (*Lesson 8 Slide 15, Lie to Me*). OB tracks **nine non-verbal modes** (*body movement/kinesics, facial expressions, eye gaze, posture, touch, spatial distance/proxemics, vocalics [pitch/pace/silence], physical appearance, artifacts*) clustering into six readable signals (*Openness, Defensiveness, Boredom/impatience, Enthusiasm, Lack of understanding, Stress*).

Two spatial laws matter directly for office and hybrid design:
1. **Edward Hall (`1963`) Proxemics (`4` Spatial Zones)**:
   - **Intimate Zone (`0–50 cm`)**: Whispering, close trust/comfort (*invasive if unsolicited*).
   - **Personal Zone (`0.5–1 m`)**: Close friends, informal check-ins.
   - **Social Zone (`1–4 m`)**: Standard professional conversations and meetings.
   - **Public Zone (`4 m+`)**: Lectures, keynote halls, speeches.
2. **Thomas Allen (`2007`, *CMR*) Distance Decay Curve & Three Technical Communication Types**:
   - Measuring weekly engineer interactions revealed **exponential decay**: probability of regular face-to-face technical communication peaks around **`0.24` (`24%`)** near `0 m`, plunges steeply beyond **`20–30 meters`**, and flattens below **`0.05`** (`40–100 m+`)! Separating R&D floors kills spontaneous innovation across **Allen's Three Types**:
     - **Type I (Coordination)**: Routine work/task alignment (*can survive distance via tools*).
     - **Type II (Information)**: Keeping up to date on technical developments.
     - **Type III (Inspiration)**: Serendipitous creative sparking & cross-pollination (*collapses sharply past ~30 m unless spaces force overlap!*).

### 8.3 Barriers, High/Low Context, Active vs. Reflective Listening
Five recurring **barriers** distort organizational communication: **Gender differences** (*report-talk vs. rapport-talk*), **Power/status dynamics** (*filtering bad news upward to avoid angering bosses*), **Physical surroundings**, **Language/jargon**, and **Cultural diversity** (*Erin Meyer's **High-Context vs. Low-Context** scale*: low-context Scandinavians/Americans prioritize explicit literal words, while high-context cultures encode meaning implicitly in hierarchy and tone).

To verify decoding accuracy, replace passive hearing with two disciplined skills (*R&J Exhibit 11.1, Lesson 8 Slide 25*):
- **Active Listening** *(Three Behavioral Steps)*: **Sensing** (staying focused without interrupting) $\to$ **Processing** (integrating words + non-verbal meaning) $\to$ **Responding** (paraphrasing & asking clarifying questions).
- **Reflective Listening** *(Deepening Understanding)*: Explicitly **acknowledging feelings**, **restating** core ideas, and **reformulating** concerns back to the speaker so they confirm *"Yes, that's what I meant!"*

### 8.4 Channel Richness, Automatic vs. Controlled Processing & Digital Media Matrix
Information processing splits between fast **Automatic Processing** (*superficial heuristics, low time, vulnerable to bias — best matched only to minor low-stakes memos*) and effortful **Controlled Processing** (*detailed critical evaluation needed for complex strategic changes*). Meanwhile, **information overload** degrades decision quality when volume exceeds processing capacity.

Match **Channel Richness** (*capacity to transmit multiple cues simultaneously, facilitate rapid feedback, and stay personal*) to task ambiguity (*Lesson 8 Slides 30–34, R&J Ch. 11 / Brodsky 2021*):

| Channel | Richness | Best Use Cases (*Lesson 8 Rules*) | Major Pitfalls |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **In-Person / Video Meetings** | **Highest** | High ambiguity, conflict, delicate persuasion, building trust, **creative Type III brainstorming** | Scheduling cost, Zoom fatigue |
| **Phone Call** | **High** | Quick clarification (`<30 min`), **emotionally sensitive or verbal nuance** lacking face-to-face logistics | No permanent written record |
| **Email** | **Medium–Low** *(Async)* | Multi-recipient updates, confirming **post-meeting decisions**, formal docs, approvals, SOPs *(Adobe survey: `40% <=1h`, `22% 1–2h`, `16% 2–4h`, `9% 4–6h`, `12% >6h`)* | Poor for conflict/emotion; tone misread coldly! |
| **IM / Slack / Text** | **Low–Medium** *(Semi-Sync)* | Brief **FYI pings**, checking live availability, **real-time co-editing**, ongoing tactical coordination | Interrupts deep focus (**techno-overload**); bad for formal accountability |

### 8.5 Change & Communication + Sources of Resistance (`R&J Ch. 16`)
As Lesson 8 puts it succinctly: ***"Change triggers fear; Communication creates trust"*** — and via **Kotter's View**: ***"People don't follow messages, they follow consistency."*** Five practical rules govern effective change communication (*illustrated by the **Elegance Inc. — CSO Elena Green** mini-case on hybrid-work anxiety*): *(1) Explain the "Why" early*, *(2) Communicate consistently across channels*, *(3) Frame relevance to employee reality*, *(4) Listen actively to fears*, and *(5) Model the change in leader behavior*.

Why do people and organizations resist change? **Robbins & Judge (`Exhibit 16-8`, Ch. 16 p. 576)** classifies resistance into:
- **Five Individual Sources**: *(1) Habit*, *(2) Security needs*, *(3) Economic factors* (fear of lower pay/productivity), *(4) Fear of the unknown*, and *(5) Selective information processing* (hearing only what defends existing views).
- **Six Organizational Sources**: *(1) Structural inertia* (selection & rules engineered for stability), *(2) Limited focus of change* (changing one subsystem gets nullified by unchanged interdependent ones), *(3) Group inertia* (peer norms), *(4) Threat to expertise* (obsolescence of specialized skills), *(5) Threat to established power relationships*, and *(6) Threat to established resource allocations*.

**Eight Tactics for Overcoming Resistance to Change** (*R&J Ch. 16 pp. 577–579 — high MCQ favorite!*):
1. **Communication**: Explaining the logic and reducing rumor-fueled fear *(framing changes fairly across stakeholders)*.
2. **Participation**: Involving affected employees who possess relevant expertise in **genuine co-design** (*harder to resist what you built — though time-consuming*).
3. **Building Support & Commitment**: Counseling, training, coaching, and building emotional attachment.
4. **Developing Positive Relationships**: High trust in change agents lowers cynicism.
5. **Implementing Changes Fairly**: **Procedural & Informational Justice** dramatically lift acceptance even of tough restructurings!
6. **Manipulation & Cooptation** *(Warning Trap!)*: **Manipulation** = covertly twisting/withholding facts or false rumors; **Cooptation** = **buying off leaders of a resisting group by giving them a symbolic key role/seat purely to get their endorsement, NOT their genuine advice**!
7. **Selecting People Who Accept Change**: Hiring high Openness / risk-tolerant individuals.
8. **Coercion**: Direct threats of termination, loss of promotion, or negative evaluations (*fast, legal/ethical risk, destroys trust*).

> [!warning] Look-Alike Trap — Participation vs. Cooptation
> Both give a critic a seat at the table! Look at **management's intent**: **Participation** genuinely seeks the employee's expertise to improve the solution; **Cooptation** hands out an impressive title or committee role **purely to buy endorsement and silence opposition**.

### 8.6 Four Approaches to Managing Planned Change (`Lewin`, `Kotter`, `Action Research`, `Appreciative Inquiry`)
1. **Kurt Lewin's Three-Step Model**:
   - **Step 1 — Unfreezing**: Overcoming status-quo equilibrium either by **increasing Driving Forces** (pushing away from status quo), **decreasing Restraining Forces** (fears/habits blocking change — *preferred because it lowers tension!*), or combining both.
   - **Step 2 — Movement**: Shifting behaviors, workflows, and structures to the target state.
   - **Step 3 — Refreezing**: Stabilizing the new state by aligning incentives, rules, and culture so behavior doesn't snap back.

2. **John Kotter's Eight-Step Plan** *(Expands Lewin directly: **Steps 1–4 = Unfreezing**, **Steps 5–7 = Movement**, **Step 8 = Refreezing**)*:
   1. Establish a **sense of urgency**.
   2. Form a **powerful guiding coalition**.
   3. Create a **new vision** and strategy.
   4. **Communicate the vision** clearly and consistently.
   5. **Empower others** to act on the vision by removing obstacles.
   6. Plan for and create **short-term wins** (credibility momentum!).
   7. Consolidate improvements and **reassess/adjust** (*don't declare victory too soon!*).
   8. **Anchor/reinforce changes** into organizational culture (*Refreezing*).

3. **Action Research**: Scientific `5`-step data-driven change cycle (*Diagnosis $\to$ Analysis $\to$ Feedback $\to$ Action $\to$ Evaluation*) involving clients collaboratively.
4. **Organizational Development & Appreciative Inquiry (`AI`)**: Rather than hunting problems/deficits (*"what's broken?"*), **Appreciative Inquiry** identifies an organization's unique **positive strengths** through four **`4-D` stages**: *Discovery* (best moments) $\to$ *Dreaming* (envisioning potential) $\to$ *Designing* (shared architecture) $\to$ *Destiny* (implementing strengths).

## 9. Lesson 9: Diversity and Creativity

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 9 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 2 & Ch. 5*)
> Lesson 9 explodes popular myths about both workplace diversity and genius creativity: **diversity only yields superior creativity (*DNB Stay Ahead case*) when leaders manage surface friction into deep-level psychological safety**, and creativity follows a structured, collaborative social process (**Wallas 4-Stage + Amabile Componential Model**).

### 9.1 Surface-Level vs. Deep-Level Diversity and Hofstede's 6 Dimensions
- **Surface-Level Diversity**: Easily observable demographic/biographical differences — *age, gender, race/ethnicity, tenure, physical disability* (*Lesson 8 Q2 & Q4!*). Initially triggers stereotyping, social categorization, and defensive conflict if mismanaged.
- **Deep-Level Diversity**: Underlying **values, personality, cognitive styles, and work preferences** (*Lesson 8 Q4!*). As teammates work together over time, **surface differences become less important while deep-level values determine trust, cohesion, and performance**!
- **Biographical Characteristics Facts (`R&J Ch. 2`)**: Empirical meta-analyses refute common myths — *older workers* show **lower avoidable absenteeism, lower turnover, equal job performance, and equal/higher OCB** (despite myths of rigidity); *tenure* positively predicts productivity and job satisfaction and negatively predicts turnover; *gender* shows **zero consistent difference in job performance**.
- **Hofstede's Full `6` Dimensions (`Lesson 9 Slide 12`)**: Builds on Lesson 2 (*Power Distance, Individualism–Collectivism, Uncertainty Avoidance, Masculinity–Femininity, Long-Term–Short-Term Orientation*) by adding **(6) Indulgence vs. Restraint** (*degree to which a society allows free gratification of basic human desires/fun vs. strict social-norm restraint*).

### 9.2 Diversity Dynamics & Managing Conflict into Performance
Why do some diverse teams outperform homogeneous ones while others implode? Lesson 9 highlights three crucial dynamics:
1. **Actual Diversity $\neq$ Perceived Diversity**: How diverse members *feel* the climate is (inclusion & fairness) drives behavior more than headcount ratios alone.
2. **Surface triggers early conflict $\to$ Deep engagement builds trust**: Diverse groups suffer **higher initial relationship/coordination friction**, yet if bridged through shared identity, generate **stronger decision quality and innovation** (*supporting McKinsey & Credit Suisse empirical findings: top-quartile ethnic diversity `+35%`, gender diversity `+15%`, combined `+25%`, board gender diversity `+26%` superior financial likelihood — correlation/context caveats noted*).
3. **Three Managerial Levers to Reduce Conflict & Boost Cohesion (`Lesson 9 Slide 14`)**:
   - **Maintain a task-focused leader** who keeps attention on objective work goals rather than personal ego.
   - **Transform *"Us vs. Them"* into *"We"*** (superordinate team identity & shared goals).
   - **Encourage meaningful intergroup contact** across faultlines so members discover deep-level commonalities.

### 9.3 Defining Creativity (`Mumford, 2003`) & Refuting the Three Myths
In OB, **creativity** is **not** eccentric art or wild impractical brainstorming. **Mumford (`2003`)** defines creativity strictly by **two joint requirements**:
$$\text{Creativity} = \text{Novelty (New / Original)} \times \text{Usefulness (Practical / Value-Creating)}$$
*(Notice: Novel without Useful = bizarre/irrelevant; Useful without Novel = routine replication; **Innovation** then implements those creative ideas into real products/processes!)*

Lesson 9 systematically debunks **three stubborn myths about creativity**:

#### Myth #1: "Creativity Comes from a Sudden Lone Eureka Moment" $\to$ Reality: `Wallas` & `Amabile`
1. **Graham Wallas (`1926`) Four-Stage Creative Process**:
   - **Stage 1 — Preparation / Recognition of Problem**: Deeply studying data, constraints, and existing solutions (*immersion*).
   - **Stage 2 — Incubation**: Stepping away mentally while unconscious associative networks recombine elements (*the value of walks, showers, or breaks after intense preparation!*).
   - **Stage 3 — Illumination**: The sudden "aha" insight surfacing into awareness.
   - **Stage 4 — Verification**: Rigorous testing, prototyping, critique, and adaptation against usefulness standards (*most ideas die or mutate here!*).
2. **Teresa Amabile (`1983`) Componential Model of Creativity (`3` Ingredients across `5` Stages)**:
   - **Domain-Relevant Skills**: Technical expertise, facts, and mastery inside the field.
   - **Creativity-Relevant Processes**: Cognitive **set-breaking** (*suspending assumptions*), risk tolerance, and **analogical thinking** (*e.g., **Pritt Stick (`1967`)** combining lipstick twist-tubes with adhesive; **sushi conveyor belts** inspiring airport luggage; **F1 pit stops** improving hospital surgery handoffs & drive-thrus; Luke Edward Hall's `4` discovery habits: **Associating, Experimenting, Networking, Observing**!*).
   - **Intrinsic Task Motivation**: Genuine curiosity and passion for solving the puzzle (*linking directly back to SDT in Lesson 12 — controlling extrinsic pressure narrows creative risk-taking!*).

#### Myth #2: "Genius Lives Isolated Inside One Hero's Brain" $\to$ Reality: The Systemic Formula
Lesson 9 quotes the **Einstein thought experiment** (born 500 years earlier or isolated in a desert, no relativity!) plus creative clusters (*1920s Paris, Silicon Valley, Hollywood*) to formalize creativity as a multiplicative ecosystem:
$$\text{Creativity} = \text{Person} \times \text{Knowledge} \times \text{Networks} \times \text{Place} \times \text{Time} \times \text{Opportunities}$$

#### Myth #3: "Homogeneous Harmony Beats Diverse Friction" $\to$ Reality: Managed Diversity (*`The Odyssey`*)
As exemplified by **DNB's *Stay Ahead*** initiative and the diverse craft crews behind Christopher Nolan's ***The Odyssey***, identical thinkers reach quick, comfortable consensus (**shallow ideas**). ***"Diversity creates potential, but you need to create the conditions for it to happen"*** — pairing cognitive/cultural variety with **Edmondson's Psychological Safety** (`Lesson 4`) and **intergroup contact**.

> [!question]- Active Recall & Look-Alike Check — Lesson 9

>    **A:** **Values** (alongside personality and work preferences); age, ethnicity, disability, and tenure are all **surface-level / biographical characteristics**.
> 2. **Q:** What two joint criteria must an idea satisfy to count as **creativity** under **Mumford (2003)**?

>    **A:** Surface differences trigger early coordination/social-categorization friction unless leaders build **task focus, shared "We" identity, and intergroup contact**, letting deep-level cognitive complementarity unlock superior **creativity**.

## 10. Lesson 10: Organizational Theory, Structure, and HR Systems

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 10 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 15 & Ch. 17*)
> Lesson 10 steps up to **Macro Organizational Design**: how organizations arrange `7` structural building blocks into archetypes (**Simple, Hierarchical, Bureaucracy, Matrix, Team, Virtual/Boundaryless**), why structures shift between **Mechanistic** and **Organic** depending on **Strategy, Size, Perrow Technology, Environment & Institutions**, and how **HR Selection & Performance Appraisal (`R&J Ch. 17`)** staff and govern those structures.

### 10.1 Seven Elements of Organizational Structure (`R&J Ch. 15`)
**Organizational structure** defines how job tasks are formally **divided, grouped, and coordinated** across **seven diagnostic elements**:

1. **Work Specialization (Division of Labor)**: Subdividing tasks into narrow, repetitive jobs (*fast-food burger assembly vs. artisan baker*). Raises efficiency up to a peak (*economies of specialization*), after which **human diseconomies** (*boredom, fatigue, stress, absenteeism, turnover — see Inverted-U in Figure 8.1a*) drive productivity back **down**!
2. **Departmentalization** *(Five bases for grouping jobs)*:
   - **Functional**: Accounting, Marketing, R&D (*economies of scale within specialties; siloed goals*).
   - **Product / Service**: Dedicated unit per product line (*clear profit accountability*).
   - **Geographical / Territory**: Nordic, DACH, Americas (*local market responsiveness*).
   - **Process**: Casting, Milling, Finishing, Packaging (*sequential flow optimization*).
   - **Customer**: Retail, Corporate, Government (*deep client tailoring*).
3. **Chain of Command**: Unbroken line of **authority** (rights inherent in a managerial position to give orders and expect obedience) from top to bottom. Traditional **Unity of Command** (*Royal Navy* model) dictates **each subordinate reports to one and only one boss** (*broken deliberately by Matrix structures!*).
4. **Span of Control**: Number of subordinates a manager can efficiently and effectively direct.
   - **Narrow span** (*e.g., `span = 4` across `4,096` workers $\to$ `7` levels, `1,365` managers*): Tight control, expensive overhead, slow vertical communication, disempowers front line.
   - **Wide span** (*e.g., `span = 8` $\to$ `5` levels, `585` managers*): Flatter, cheaper, empowers employee autonomy — demands heavy **training and clear goals** so managers aren't overwhelmed (*Company A vs. Company B slide*).
5. **Centralization vs. Decentralization**: Degree to which **decision-making** is concentrated at a single top point (**Centralized**) vs. pushed down close to the action (**Decentralized** — faster response, richer local input, lower executive overload, higher motivation).
6. **Formalization**: Degree to which jobs are standardized by explicit rules and procedures.
   - **Critical Exam Trap (*Lesson 10 Slides 32–33*)**: **High work specialization does NOT automatically mean high formalization!** A biotech research scientist has **very high specialization** yet **low formalization** (*freedom in *how* to solve puzzles*); a fast-food worker faces **high formalization** telling both **what** and **how** to cook every fry!
7. **Boundary Spanning (`Internal & External`)**: Building relationships *across* functional silos inside the firm or across outside stakeholders/ecosystems (*e.g., **Espoo, Finland** municipal innovation ecosystem led by Harri Paananen connecting city, startups, and universities*).

### 10.2 Classic & Contemporary Organizational Designs (`Matrix vs. Team` & `Bureaucracy vs. Hierarchical`)
Compare the six major designs tested in Lesson 10 and *R&J Ch. 15*:
- **Simple (Flat) Structure**: Low departmentalization, wide spans, **authority centralized in one owner**, minimal formalization (*fast, flexible, cheap for startups — collapses past ~50–100 staff, as seen in **NordTech (`40 -> 600` employees)**!*).
- **Traditional Hierarchical Structure**: Clear single chain of command, vertical pyramids, predictable functional silos (*clear accountability, yet slow and political across silos*).
- **Bureaucracy (`Max Weber`)**: Defined by **standardization** (*high formalization, functional departments, centralized authority, narrow spans, rule-bound promotions*). Compare carefully: *Hierarchical* emphasizes **top-down personal/rank chain**, whereas *Bureaucracy* emphasizes **impersonal standardized rules, procedures, and merit/credential routines** so anyone can be swapped into a role!
- **Matrix Structure**: Combines **Functional** and **Product** departmentalization simultaneously $\implies$ **dual chain of command (`2` bosses — directly breaks Unity of Command!)**. (*InnovateCo* case: great cross-silo talent pooling, yet generates **role ambiguity, power struggles, and stress** unless communication is disciplined!).
- **Team Structure (`Pixar` async case; Coca-Cola / McDonald's)**: Uses decentralized self-managed cross-functional teams as the **core organizing device**, breaking vertical, horizontal, and external barriers.

| Design Criterion *(Lesson 10 Slide 17)* | Matrix Structure | Team Structure |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Authority** | **Dual authority** (*Functional boss + Project boss*) | **Shared / Decentralized** team autonomy |
| **Coordination** | Formal cross-reporting lines & meetings | Direct **peer collaboration** across roles |
| **Decision Speed** | Often **slower** (bosses must negotiate conflicts) | **Faster** (*empowered near the customer/problem*) |
| **Primary Purpose** | Pool specialized experts efficiently across multiple projects | Maximize **agility, innovation & shared ownership** |

- **Virtual (Network / Modular) Organization**: Small core hub outsourcing major functions (*manufacturing, logistics, marketing*) to independent partners (`R&J Exhibit 15-6`, *Dell modular parts*) $\implies$ maximum flexibility, minimal overhead, lower employee loyalty/control.
- **Circular & Boundaryless Organizations (`R&J Ch. 15`)**: Circular places top executives at the center radiating vision outward rather than top-down; Boundaryless removes internal vertical/horizontal chains and blurs external supplier/customer walls.

### 10.3 Strategy, Size, Perrow Technology, Environment & Mechanistic–Organic Fit
Why should **NordTech** redesign itself differently from an oil refinery? Organizations span between two extreme poles (*Figure 10.1a*):
- **Mechanistic Model**: High specialization, rigid departmentalization, clear chain of command, narrow spans, centralization, high formalization.
- **Organic Model**: Cross-functional/hierarchical teams, low formalization, comprehensive lateral information networks, wide spans, decentralized participation.

**Five Structural Determinants (`R&J Ch. 15 pp. 535–541` + Sample Exam Q10)**:
1. **Strategy (`Structure follows Strategy`)**:
   - **Innovation Strategy** (major breakthroughs: *Tesla, Netflix*) $\implies$ **Organic** (*low specialization/formalization, decentralized*).
   - **Cost-Minimization Strategy** (tight cost controls, price cutting: *Walmart, Ryanair*) $\implies$ **Mechanistic** (*high control, centralized, formal rules*).
   - **Imitation Strategy** (moves into proven markets safely) $\implies$ **Hybrid** (*mechanistic controls over core lines + organic R&D/launch subunits*).
2. **Organization Size**: Large organizations (`2,000+` employees) are systematically more specialized, departmentalized, vertical, and rule-bound — *with diminishing marginal impact past ~2,000* (*adding 500 staff to a `300`-person firm forces massive mechanistic restructuring!*).
3. **Technology & Charles Perrow's (`1967`) Typology (`Sample Exam Q10!`)**: How the organization transfers inputs into outputs shapes structure. **R&J (`Ch. 15`)** contrasts **Routine** technologies (*automated, standardized $\to$ tall/mechanistic/centralized unless extreme formalization permits slightly wider control*) vs. **Nonroutine** technologies (*custom, uncertain $\to$ organic*). **Perrow's `2×2` Model** sharpens this across **Task Variability** (*frequency of exceptions*) $\times$ **Problem Analyzability** (*clear step-by-step analytical procedures vs. intuition/judgment*):

| Perrow Typology (`Sample Exam Q10`) | Low Task Variability *(Few Exceptions)* | High Task Variability *(Many Exceptions)* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Analyzable Problems** *(Objective procedures)* | **1. Routine** *(Assembly lines, bank tellers $\to$ **Mechanistic**)* | **2. Engineering** *(Heavy machinery, accounting/legal prep $\to$ Flexible/professionalized)* |
| **Unanalyzable Problems** *(Judgment/experience needed)* | **3. Craft** *(Specialty glassblowing, bespoke carpentry $\to$ Decentralized expertise)* | **4. Nonroutine** *(Aerospace R&D, basic biotech, strategic consulting $\to$ **Organic**!)* |

4. **Environment (`3D Model`, *R&J Exhibit 15-10*)**: Evaluated across **Capacity** (*Abundant vs. Scarce*), **Volatility** (*Stable vs. Dynamic*), and **Complexity** (*Simple vs. Complex*). **Scarce + Dynamic + Complex** environments generate maximum uncertainty $\implies$ require **Organic** agility; **Abundant + Stable + Simple** environments suit **Mechanistic** efficiency!
5. **Institutions**: Regulatory/cultural norms press firms into look-alike structures (*institutional isomorphism*) even when non-adaptive (*note also **downsizing** harms both victims and "survivors" via stress and voluntary turnover unless cushioned by open communication and participation!*).

### 10.4 Human Resource Systems & Selection Bridge (`R&J Ch. 17`)
Structure only executes through **HR Systems (`R&J Ch. 17 pp. 594–616`)** — especially how firms **select**, **train**, and **evaluate** employees:
- **Initial $\to$ Substantive $\to$ Contingent Selection**: Resume/application blanks screen basic eligibility (**Initial**); substantive tests verify ability (**Substantive**); medical/drug/background checks verify final conditions (**Contingent**).
- **Substantive Selection Methods (`R&J Ch. 17 pp. 599–603`)**:
  - **Written Tests**: **Intelligence / Cognitive Ability tests** are the **#1 single best predictor of job performance across almost all jobs** (*especially complex cognitive work*); supplemented by **Personality (`Big Five`)** and **Integrity** tests (*unpopular with applicants who prefer interviews/simulations*).
  - **Performance-Simulation Tests**: High face & predictive validity because candidates *do* the work — **Work Sample Tests** (hands-on replicas), **Assessment Centers** (*1–several day managerial in-basket & role-play evaluations*), and **Situational Judgment Tests (`SJTs`)** (cheaper scenario benchmarks compared against top performers).
  - **Structured vs. Unstructured Interviews**: **Unstructured interviews** suffer heavily from similarity bias, contrast effects, and `5`-minute first impressions; **Structured interviews** (standardized behavioral/situational questions + anchored scoring rubrics) double predictive validity!
- **Performance Evaluation, EPM & Recovery (`R&J pp. 612–615`)**: **Electronic Performance Monitoring (`EPM`)** tracks login/keystrokes to curb cyberloafing yet spikes stress unless seen as fair. Rater biases (*stereotypes evaluating minorities on errors rather than potential, leniency, halo*) drop when using **multiple evaluators (`360-degree`), specific behavior checklists, and clear criteria**. Finally, **R&J Box `p. 615`** (*tested directly in Official Tech Q2!*) stresses **after-hours smartphone/recovery policies**: constant late-night work emails trigger **work–family conflict and psychological strain**, making uninterrupted **recovery time** essential for long-term performance!

## 11. Lesson 11: Technology, Algorithmic Management, and Work

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 11 (`Aspø` | *Lecture 11 + Brynjolfsson, Mazmanian, Bernstein, Kellogg, Rahman*)
> Lesson 11 explains **why software, smartphones, and AI rarely deliver the straightforward autonomy or productivity gains managers promise**. Notice this topic carries **4 dedicated Official Exam Practice Questions (`T1–T4`)** testing **Mazmanian's Autonomy Paradox**, **R&J Ch. 17 smartphone recovery (`p. 615`)**, **Rahman's Invisible Cage**, and **AI job-polarization/re-skilling**!

### 11.1 Technological Determinism vs. Sociomateriality (`Orlikowski`)
A fundamental mistake in management is **Technological Determinism** — assuming that dropping a new tool (*Slack, Copilot, CRM software*) automatically forces a predictable human behavior. Instead, OB relies on **Social Shaping / Sociomateriality**: **technologies offer possibilities (*affordances*), yet organizational outcomes depend on how humans, norms, incentives, and power relations actually use and enforce them in practice**.

### 11.2 Productivity J-Curve, Autonomy Paradox (`Mazmanian`), and Transparency Paradox (`Bernstein`)
Three empirically famous workplace paradoxes sit at the heart of Lesson 11 (*see Figure 11.1*):

1. **Solow Computer Paradox & Brynjolfsson's Productivity J-Curve (`Figure 11.1a`)**:
   - Robert Solow (`1987`) famously quipped: *"You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."*
   - **Brynjolfsson, Rock & Syverson** explained why with the **Productivity J-Curve**: general-purpose technologies (`IT`, `AI`) initially **depress measured productivity** (*dip of the `J`*) because organizations must spend years building **intangible organizational complements** — redesigned workflows, new decision rights, skills training, and decentralized processes — before massive harvest gains erupt!

2. **Mazmanian, Orlikowski & Yates (`2013`) — The Autonomy Paradox (`Official Tech Q1 & Figure 11.1b`)**:
   - Studying knowledge-worker professionals (*corporate lawyers & consultants*) adopting mobile email devices, Mazmanian et al. uncovered a painful cycle:
     1. Professionals **voluntarily chose** mobile email to boost personal **flexibility** (*leaving the office earlier, checking messages from home*).
     2. Replying quickly signaled dedication and competence, gradually resetting **collective social expectations**: peers and clients began assuming **constant `24/7` availability**.
     3. Escalating responsiveness turned an optional tool into a **collective norm of continuous availability**, trapping everyone with **less collective autonomy, higher stress, and impaired work–life boundaries**!
   - *(Compare **R&J Ch. 17 p. 615** & **Official Tech Q2**: organizations must enforce explicit disconnect/recovery policies — because late-night smartphone usage destroys restorative sleep and elevates strain even when workers claim they "chose" to check emails!)*

3. **Ethan Bernstein (`2012`) — The Transparency Paradox**:
   - Intuitively, removing walls and adding continuous digital/line-of-sight monitoring should improve productivity. In a huge Chinese electronics factory study, Bernstein found the opposite: **total observability forced workers into performative compliance and *hiding behavior*** (*covering up smarter local shortcuts behind curtains or reverting to slow textbook steps whenever bosses watched*), **killing local experimentation and learning**! Protected zones of **privacy** actually *raised* factory output!

### 11.3 Kellogg's `6 R's`, The Invisible Cage (`Rahman, 2021`), and The Pacifying Algorithm (`Rahman et al., 2024`)
How do platforms (*Uber, Upwork, Amazon warehouses*) and AI software manage thousands of dispersed workers without human middle managers?

1. **Kellogg, Valentine & Christin (`2020`) — Algorithmic Control via the `6 R's`**:
   | Control Function | Traditional Bureaucratic Mechanism | Algorithmic `2 R's` Pair |
   | :--- | :--- | :--- |
   | **Algorithmic Direction** *(what to do, in what order)* | Written SOPs & supervisor orders | **Restricting** (limiting options/visibility) & **Recommending** (prompts, surge pricing, nudges) |
   | **Algorithmic Evaluation** *(how performance is judged)* | Annual appraisals & visual checks | **Recording** (fine-grained telemetry/clicks) & **Rating** (automated score aggregation & rankings) |
   | **Algorithmic Discipline** *(enforcing compliance)* | Warnings, bonuses, firing | **Replacing** (automated deactivation/un-scheduling) & **Rewarding** (dynamic tiers/bonuses) |

2. **Hatim Rahman (`2021`) — *The Invisible Cage* (`Official Tech Q3`)**:
   - Studying high-skilled freelancers on an online talent platform, Rahman asked: *why do workers obey strict discipline when the platform doesn't publish clear rules?*
   - **Mechanism**: The platform relies on **opaque, continuously shifting evaluation algorithms** (*a hidden Job Success Score*). Because workers **cannot see exact weights or thresholds**, yet suffer severe income penalties if their score drops, they experience chronic uncertainty and respond through **reactive guesswork, extreme risk-aversion, accepting unfair client demands silently, and over-constraining their own behavior** — trapped inside an **"Invisible Cage"** far stricter than transparent rules!

3. **Rahman, Weiss & Karunakaran (`2024`) — *The Pacifying Algorithm***:
   - Why don't platform workers unionize or revolt against opaque shifts? Platforms deploy **experimental algorithmic updates** while **framing them rhetorically as benign, protective, data-driven *"tests"*** (*"we are tweaking matching to protect marketplace fairness/newcomers"*). By masking managerial control as neutral technical experimentation (**pacifying** frustration into patient waiting), platforms **prevent collective blame and neutralize worker resistance**!

### 11.4 AI Augmentation vs. Automation & Techno-Stress (`Official Tech Q4`)
As generative AI enters knowledge work (**R&J & Brynjolfsson/Erik Brynjolfsson** frameworks; **Official Tech Q4**):
- **Automation** replaces routine codifiable tasks cleanly, **polarizing** job markets or threatening routine clerical roles unless firms invest in **re-skilling**.
- **Augmentation** pairs AI pattern/drafting speed with **human judgment, empathy, ethical accountability, and contextual framing** (*requiring continuous learning and adaptive structures rather than layoffs*).
- **Techno-Stress** introduces three distinct digital strains: **Techno-Overload** (faster/longer work forced by tech alerts), **Techno-Invasion** (work bleeding into evenings/vacations — *cf. Autonomy Paradox*), and **Techno-Insecurity** (fear of AI displacement).

## 12. Lesson 12: Motivation, Job Design, and Organizational Justice

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 12 (`Aspø` | *R&J 19e Ch. 7 & Ch. 8*)
> Lesson 12 unites **why people exert effort (`Ch. 7`: Early Needs, SDT, Goal-Setting, Self-Efficacy, Reinforcement, Equity & 4-Way Justice, Expectancy)** with **how jobs and pay can be engineered (`Ch. 8`: Hackman & Oldham JCM `MPS`, Job Enrichment vs. Enlargement, Relational Job Design, Variable Pay)**. Pay careful attention to the exact multiplicative traps in **Vroom (`E × I × V`)** and **JCM (`MPS`)** plus **Lesson 12 Slide 51 Justice scenarios**!

### 12.1 Defining Motivation & Early Needs Theories (`Maslow`, `Herzberg`, `McClelland`)
**Motivation** is defined rigorously as the processes that account for an individual's **intensity** (how hard a person tries), **direction** (channeled constructively toward organizational goals), and **persistence** (how long effort is sustained) toward attaining a goal (*tested verbatim in Lesson 8 Q5!*).

Three historical **Content / Needs Theories** explain *what* inner needs activate behavior:
1. **Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs**: Five stacked steps — *Physiological $\to$ Safety–Security $\to$ Social–Belongingness $\to$ Esteem $\to$ Self-Actualization*. **OB Critique**: Useful descriptive metaphor, yet **lacks empirical support** for a rigid step-by-step ladder (cultures vary and multiple needs operate simultaneously).
2. **Herzberg's Two-Factor (Motivation–Hygiene) Theory** *(Sample Exam Q4!)*:
   - **Critical Counter-Intuitive Discovery**: **The opposite of Job Satisfaction is NOT Job Dissatisfaction — it is *No Dissatisfaction* (neutral)!** Removing terrible conditions prevents misery without creating active motivation!
   - **Hygiene Factors** *(Extrinsic work context: **pay**, company policy, physical working conditions, relationship with supervisor, job security)* $\to$ Fixing hygiene moves workers from *Dissatisfied $\to$ Neutral*.
   - **Motivators** *(Intrinsic job content: **achievement, recognition, work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth**)* $\to$ Supplying motivators moves workers from *Neutral $\to$ Satisfied & Motivated*!
3. **McClelland's Theory of Needs (`3` Learned Needs)**:
   - **Need for Achievement (`nAch`)**: Drive to excel and succeed against standards; seeks personal responsibility, **rapid feedback**, and **moderate (`50/50`) calculated risk** (*avoids both boringly easy tasks and pure lottery odds!*). **Classic Trap**: **High `nAch` employees make brilliant solo contributors/entrepreneurs, NOT automatically great senior executives** (because they want personal credit rather than influencing through others!).
   - **Need for Power (`nPow`)**: Desire to make others behave in ways they otherwise wouldn't (*Institutional/Socialized nPow* builds org goals vs. *Personalized nPow* seeks ego dominance).
   - **Need for Affiliation (`nAff`)**: Desire for friendly, close interpersonal harmony (*best top managers combine **High Institutional `nPow` + Low `nAff`** so they can make tough fair decisions without begging to be liked!).*

### 12.2 Contemporary Process & Cognitive Theories (`SDT`, `Goal-Setting`, `Self-Efficacy`)
Modern OB shifts from static needs to **cognitive mechanisms**:

1. **Self-Determination Theory (`SDT`, `Deci & Ryan`) & Cognitive Evaluation Theory**:
   - Humans thrive when work satisfies three innate psychological needs: **Autonomy** (self-endorsed choice), **Competence** (mastery), and **Relatedness** (meaningful social connection).
   - **Cognitive Evaluation / Overjustification Effect**: Introducing **tangible, controlling extrinsic rewards** (*"We'll pay you `\$5` for every book you already loved reading"*) shifts the perceived locus of causality outside the self and **undermines (crowds out) intrinsic motivation** once rewards stop — whereas **verbal praise & autonomy-supportive feedback** *enhance* intrinsic drive!
   - **Self-Concordance / Internalization Continuum**: *Amotivation $\to$ External Regulation* (carrots/sticks) $\to$ *Introjected* (guilt/ego) $\to$ *Identified* (personally valued goal) $\to$ *Integrated* $\to$ **Intrinsic Motivation** (pure joy in task).

2. **Locke & Latham Goal-Setting Theory** *(Among the highest empirical validity theories in all of OB!)*:
   - Core propositions:
     1. **Specific goals** produce vastly higher performance than vague *"do your best"* encouragement.
     2. **Difficult (challenging) goals**, when **accepted**, yield higher output than easy goals.
     3. **Feedback** — especially **self-generated feedback** — amplifies goal performance significantly.
   - **Three Contingency Moderators**: *Goal commitment* (strongest when goals are **public, internal locus of control, self-set or fairly explained**), *Task complexity* (simpler learned tasks benefit fastest; complex novel tasks need strategy learning first), and *National culture*.
   - Also distinguish **Promotion Focus** (*striving for advancement/aspirations*) vs. **Prevention Focus** (*avoiding losses/fulfilling duties*) and **Management by Objectives (`MBO`)** (*cascading participatively set, tangible, verifiable goals with explicit time windows and performance feedback*).

3. **Bandura's Self-Efficacy Theory (Social Cognitive Theory)**:
   - **Self-Efficacy** is an individual's belief that **they are capable of performing a specific task** (*distinct from global self-esteem!*). Note the **Pygmalion / Galatea loop**: high expectations spark higher efficacy $\to$ persistence through setbacks!
   - **Four Sources of Self-Efficacy (Ranked)**:
     1. **Enactive Mastery** *(Most powerful!* — actually succeeding at progressive real tasks).
     2. **Vicarious Modeling** (*seeing a similar peer succeed*).
     3. **Verbal Persuasion** (*credible coaching — Pygmalion!*).
     4. **Arousal** (*energized physical readiness — vs. panic*).

### 12.3 Reinforcement, Equity Theory & Four-Way Organizational Justice (`Slide 51`)
1. **Operant Conditioning / Reinforcement Theory (`Skinner`)**: Behavior is environmentally shaped by consequences rather than inner cognitive states:
   - **Positive Reinforcement**: Follow desired behavior with a pleasant reward (*bonus for zero defects*).
   - **Negative Reinforcement**: Follow desired behavior by **removing an unpleasant stimulus** (*stopping daily supervisor check-ins once a sales rep hits quota!* — **NOT Punishment!**).
   - **Punishment**: Follow *undesired* behavior with an unpleasant consequence (*docking pay for tardiness*).
   - **Extinction**: Eliminate any prior reward maintaining a behavior (*ignoring constant jokes/complaints so they fade*).

2. **Adams' Equity Theory**: Employees evaluate fairness by comparing their **Outcome-to-Input ratio** against a **Referent** (*Self-inside, Self-outside, Other-inside, Other-outside*):
   $$\frac{\text{Outcomes}_A}{\text{Inputs}_A} \;\text{vs.}\; \frac{\text{Outcomes}_B}{\text{Inputs}_B}$$
   When workers perceive **underpayment inequity** ($\frac{O_A}{I_A} < \frac{O_B}{I_B}$), tension motivates **six behavioral/cognitive reactions**: *(1) Change inputs (slack off — exert less effort)*, *(2) Change outcomes (negotiate raise or produce higher piece-rate quantity at lower quality)*, *(3) Distort perceptions of self*, *(4) Distort perceptions of referent*, *(5) Choose a different referent*, or *(6) Leave the field (quit)*.

3. **Organizational Justice (`Four Distinct Dimensions` — *Lesson 12 Slide 51 Exercises!*)**:
   Modern OB extends equity into a comprehensive `4`-part fairness audit:
   - **Distributive Justice**: Perceived fairness of the **outcome/allocation itself** (*"Did I receive a fair bonus/grade relative to peers?"*).
   - **Procedural Justice**: Perceived fairness of the **process and rules** used to determine outcomes (**voice**, bias suppression, consistency, appeal mechanisms — *"Even though I lost the promotion, the scoring criteria were transparent and I got a fair hearing!"*).
   - **Interpersonal Justice**: Degree to which employees are treated with **dignity, politeness, and respect** by authorities (*or insulted/humiliated!*).
   - **Informational Justice**: Degree to which authorities provide **honest, candid, timely explanations** explaining *why* procedures were used or *why* outcomes turned out a certain way.
   *(Remember Lesson 12's classic empirical finding: when outcomes are harsh [e.g., pay cuts], high **Procedural + Interpersonal + Informational Justice** dramatically slashes retaliation/theft!)*

### 12.4 Vroom's Expectancy Theory (`M = E × I × V`)
**Victor Vroom's Expectancy Theory** predicts motivation from **three multiplicative perceptions** (*Figure 7.1b*):
$$\text{Motivation} = \text{Expectancy } (E) \times \text{Instrumentality } (I) \times \text{Valence } (V)$$
1. **Expectancy (`Effort → Performance`)**: *"If I give maximum effort, will I actually perform well?"* (*Requires ability, clear goals, self-efficacy, and fair evaluation*).
2. **Instrumentality (`Performance → Reward`)**: *"If I perform well, will the organization actually deliver the promised reward?"* (*Requires trust — shattered by political favoritism or shifting goalposts!*).
3. **Valence (`Reward → Personal Goals`)**: *"Do I personally value the reward being offered?"* (*A `\$500` coffee-shop gift card holds near-zero Valence for someone needing flexible childcare hours!*).

**Exam Golden Rule (`Zero-Veto Multiplication`)**: Because $E$, $I$, and $V$ **multiply** together, **if ANY ONE link drops near zero, total motivation collapses to ZERO** (*even if the bonus is huge [$V \gg 0$], an exhausted employee who believes the target is impossible [$E \approx 0$] puts in zero extra effort!*).

### 12.5 Job Characteristics Model (`JCM`) & Applied Job Design (`R&J Ch. 8`)
How do managers redesign boring jobs to unleash intrinsic motivation (*Herzberg's motivators + SDT autonomy*)? **Hackman & Oldham's Job Characteristics Model (`JCM`, *Figure 12.1a*)** specifies **five core job dimensions** flowing through **three critical psychological states**:
- **Skill Variety (`SV`)**, **Task Identity (`TI`, whole piece of work from start to finish)**, **Task Significance (`TS`, meaningful impact on others)** $\longrightarrow$ *Experienced Meaningfulness of Work*.
- **Autonomy (`AU`, freedom/discretion in scheduling & methods)** $\longrightarrow$ *Experienced Responsibility for Outcomes*.
- **Feedback (`FB`, direct clear info from the job itself)** $\longrightarrow$ *Knowledge of Actual Results*.

Compute the **Motivating Potential Score (`MPS`)** exactly using:
$$\text{MPS} = \left(\frac{\text{SV} + \text{TI} + \text{TS}}{3}\right) \times \text{Autonomy} \times \text{Feedback}$$

Notice the algebra: `SV`, `TI`, and `TS` **average** together (one can compensate partially for another), whereas **Autonomy (`AU`) and Feedback (`FB`) multiply**! Thus, **if either Autonomy or Feedback is zero, `MPS = 0`** regardless of how heroic or varied the job looks! Remember **Growth-Need Strength (`GNS`)** moderates the final payoff: high-GNS individuals flourish under high `MPS`, whereas low-GNS workers can feel overwhelmed.

Compare four practical job/reward interventions from *R&J Ch. 8*:
- **Job Rotation**: Periodic shifting of an employee from one specialized task to another (*reduces boredom, builds cross-training — still leaves individual tasks narrow*).
- **Job Enlargement**: **Horizontal loading** — adding more tasks at the *same* skill/responsibility level (*weak impact on intrinsic motivation!*).
- **Job Enrichment**: **Vertical loading** — expanding **autonomy, control over planning/execution, client relationships, and direct feedback** (*raises `MPS` substantially!*).
- **Relational Job Design (`Adam Grant`)**: Connecting employees directly with end-beneficiaries (*scholarship recipients meeting university call-center fundraisers raised call pledges sharply!* — boosts **Task Significance** & prosocial motivation).
- **Variable Pay & Benefits (`Piece-rate, Merit pay, Profit-sharing, Gainsharing, ESOPs, Flexible Benefits`)**: Link rewards cleanly (`Instrumentality`) while keeping **Cognitive Evaluation** in mind so incentives don't undermine intrinsic craftsmanship.

## 13. Lesson 13: Decision Making, Emotions, and Organizational Learning

(2) How do emotions and moods shape choices (**Affective Events Theory**)? (3) Why do individuals and organizations repeat mistakes instead of learning (**4 Core Biases + Sunk Costs + Organizational Learning Formula**)?*

### 13.1 Rational, Bounded Rationality (`Satisficing`), and Intuitive Models
Walk through the **Master's University Decision (`Universities A, B, C`)** weighted scoring table from Lesson 13:

| Criterion & Weight | University A | University B *(Good Enough First Found)* | University C *(Highest Weighted Total)* |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Reputation (`0.40`) | `3` | `4` | `4` |
| Location (`0.35`) | `4` | `3` | `4` |
| Cost (`0.25`) | `3` | `4` | `4` (or `3.6`) |
| **Weighted Total** | **`3.45`** | **`3.70`** | **`3.90` (Best)** |

1. **The Rational Decision-Making Model (`Maximizing`)**: Assumes complete information, clear goals, known criteria weights, exhaustive scoring of all alternatives, and no time/cost limits across **6 steps**: *(1) Define problem $\to$ (2) Identify decision criteria $\to$ (3) Allocate weights $\to$ (4) Develop alternatives $\to$ (5) Evaluate each against every criterion $\to$ (6) Select the highest-scoring option* (**University `C`, `3.90`**).
2. **Bounded Rationality (`Herbert Simon`, Nobel Prize)**: Because real managers face **limited time, incomplete information, and bounded cognitive processing capacity**, they construct simplified models extracting essential features and **Satisfice** — seeking a solution that is ***"satisfactory and sufficient"*** (*the **first option meeting minimum threshold criteria**, e.g., **University `B`, `3.70`** without searching endlessly for `C`!*).
3. **Intuitive Decision-Making**: An unconscious process distilled from experience, rapid holistic pattern recognition, and emotional signals (*can happen to land on `C` too — remember Lesson 13 Slide 10's key insight: **different decision models can yield either the same choice or different choices**!*). Works best **only** in domains with repeated valid feedback (*fire commanders, chess masters*), and fails dangerously when paired with unchecked bias!

### 13.2 Emotions in Decision Making & Affective Events Theory (`AET`)
Contrary to folk wisdom, **emotions are NOT the opposite of rationality** (*Damasio / R&J Ch. 4 & Lesson 13*): *fear alerts us to hidden risk*, *excitement energizes persistence*, and patients with damaged emotional brain regions actually get **paralyzed** unable to weigh simple trade-offs! Destructive errors arise only when unchecked **anger, panic, or impulsiveness** hijack appraisal.
**Affective Events Theory (`AET`)** links workplace triggers straight to decisions (*Figure 12.1c*):
$$\text{Work Environment} \to \text{Daily Hassles / Uplifts (Work Events)} \to \text{Emotional Reactions} \to \begin{cases} \text{Affect-Driven Behavior (impulsive exit/helping)} \\ \text{Job Satisfaction} \to \text{Judgment-Driven Behavior} \end{cases}$$

### 13.3 Cognitive Biases and Sunk Cost Escalation (`Lesson 13` + `R&J Ch. 6`)
Lesson 13 drills **four core cognitive biases** with unforgettable concrete examples (*plus 5 textbook siblings in `R&J Ch. 6`*):

1. **Anchoring Bias**: Tendency to fixate on initial information (*the anchor*) and fail to adjust adequately afterward (*e.g., sneakers marked `NOK 2,500` vs. `NOK 1,300` crossed out $\to$ `NOK 1,200` sale feels huge only relative to the `2,500` anchor!*).
2. **Confirmation Bias**: Selective perception in action — actively seeking data that **reaffirms past choices/beliefs** while discounting disconfirming evidence.
   - *Lesson 13 Alex Case*: To test *"Is Alex unreliable?"*, Option `B` (checking objective deadlines across tasks) tests the hypothesis vs. Option `A` (asking only about missed meetings — **Confirmation Bias!**).
   - *Lesson 13 Sarah Case*: Manager labels *Sarah* as careless after **one** late arrival and ignores **three** ahead-of-schedule deliveries + mentoring a peer!
3. **Overconfidence Bias & The Dunning–Kruger Effect**: Excessive faith in our own accuracy (*Lesson 13 trivia quiz*: `Canberra` capital, `3` octopus hearts, `1989` Berlin Wall — **"Confidence $\neq$ Accuracy"**!). On the **Dunning–Kruger Curve**, novices with tiny knowledge surge onto **"Mount Stupid"** with maximum overconfidence, drop into the *"Valley of Despair"* as competence reveals complexity, and finally build calibrated expertise. *(Classic comic proof: **1995 Lemon Juice Bank Robber McArthur Wheeler**, who rubbed lemon juice on his face assuming invisible ink would hide him from security cameras — *"But I wore the juice!"*)*
4. **Escalation of Commitment / Sunk Cost Fallacy**: Staying committed to a failing decision **despite clear negative evidence**, because decision-makers refuse to admit past resources (**sunk costs**) were wasted (*e.g., **Concorde** supersonic jet funded decades past commercial viability; staying in a hated `2`-year degree solely to avoid "wasting" years already spent; **Lesson 13 Startup Case**: refusing to pivot after spending `6 months / NOK 500,000` with only `1 month / NOK 100,000` cash remaining!*).

Also recognize these **5 additional R&J Ch. 6 biases** in MCQ distractors:
- **Availability Bias**: Basing judgments on information **readily available in memory** (*recent dramatic events or vivid disasters weigh too heavily*).
- **Representativeness Bias**: Assessing likelihood by matching superficial stereotypes rather than **base rates** (*e.g., assuming quiet library-goers must be librarians*).
- **Randomness Error**: Inventing superstitious causal patterns inside random chance.
- **Risk Aversion (`Prospect Theory`)**: Preferring a sure moderate gain over a riskier gamble with higher expected value — yet **seeking huge risk to avoid locking in a sure loss** (*explaining Escalation of Commitment!*).
- **Hindsight Bias**: Believing falsely **after knowing the outcome** (*"I knew it all along!"*) that one accurately predicted it — which blocks honest post-mortem learning!

### 13.4 Why Experience $\neq$ Learning (`4 Barriers` & `Learning Formula`)
Why do smart executives repeat identical strategic blunders? Because **raw tenure (`Experience`) alone does NOT generate learning**! Lesson 13 identifies **four structural barriers**:
1. **Unclear or Delayed Feedback**: Long lag between action and result obscures what actually worked.
2. **Immediate Short-Term Rewards**: Shortcuts that pay off this quarter punish systemic truth-telling.
3. **Social Influence & Conformity**: Teams conceal errors to look competent (**Low Psychological Safety**!).
4. **Self-Justification & Ego Defense**: Blaming external luck (**Self-Serving Bias**) protects ego at the cost of insight.

Real **Organizational Learning** therefore requires all four terms together (*plus **Argyris & Schön**: **Single-Loop Learning** corrects errors using existing rules vs. **Double-Loop Learning** questions underlying assumptions/norms!*):
$$\text{Organizational Learning} = \text{Experience} + \text{Accurate Feedback} + \text{Honest Reflection} + \text{Behavioral Change}$$

## 14. Lesson 14: Conflict, Power, Politics, and Negotiation

> [!abstract] Chapter Roadmap — Lesson 14 (`De Molli` | *R&J 19e Ch. 13 & Ch. 14*)
> Lesson 14 closes the semester by showing how **interdependent groups with competing goals** navigate friction (**Conflict Types, 5-Stage Process, Thomas–Kilmann Styles**), mobilize leverage (**5 Power Bases, Dependence Postulate, 9 Influence Tactics, Politics vs. Voice/Silence**), and resolve shared resource claims (**Distributive vs. Integrative Bargaining & BATNA**).

### 14.1 Defining Conflict, Functional vs. Dysfunctional, and `3` Conflict Types
**Conflict** begins whenever **one party perceives that another party has negatively affected, or is about to negatively affect, something that the first party cares about** (*R&J Ch. 14*). Notice views evolved from **Traditional** (*all conflict = bad/irrational*) $\to$ **Interactionist** (*a minimum level keeps groups self-critical and creative*) $\to$ **Managed / Resolution-Focused** (*conflict happens naturally; minimize destructive fallout early!*).
- **Functional (Constructive) Conflict**: Supports group goals and improves decision quality (*e.g., **Emma** warning the team near deadline about a genuine technical flaw*).
- **Dysfunctional (Destructive) Conflict**: Hinders group performance through hostility, shutdown, or gridlock (*e.g., how that **`10:24` Slack message** got misread as personal disrespect — reminder: perception turns neutral facts into heated conflict!*).

Using **The Twitter Ultimatum (`2022` — Musk `"hardcore"` shift)**, Lesson 14 distinguishes **three distinct loci/types of conflict**:

| Conflict Type | Core Focus | Impact on Performance (*R&J & Lesson 14*) | Twitter `2022` Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Task Conflict** | *What* to achieve: content, goals, strategy trade-offs | **Functional when low-to-moderate** & backed by psych safety/trust! | *Employee A*: Disagrees over **speed vs. product quality** |
| **2. Process Conflict** | *How* work gets done: roles, schedules, delegation | Almost always **dysfunctional** if sustained (keep **low**!) | *Employee B*: Disagrees over **long hours & workflow org** |
| **3. Relationship Conflict** | Interpersonal tension, animosity, disrespect | **Virtually ALWAYS dysfunctional** (clashes egos & blocks listening) | *Employee C*: Feels personal **distrust & disrespect** |

### 14.2 Robbins & Judge Five-Stage Conflict Process & Thomas–Kilmann Styles
Conflict unfolds dynamically across **five stages** (*R&J Exhibit 14-1, Lesson 14 Slide 12*):
1. **Stage I — Potential Opposition / Incompatibility**: Antecedent triggers via *Communication* (noise/jargon), *Structure* (size, role ambiguity, zero-sum rewards), or *Personal Variables* (values, personality).
2. **Stage II — Cognition and Personalization**: Conflict turns real when **Perceived** (*cognitive awareness*) and especially **Felt** (*emotional tension/anxiety — shapes intentions!*).
3. **Stage III — Intentions**: Strategic choices between **Assertiveness** (satisfying *own* concerns) and **Cooperativeness** (satisfying *other's* concerns — **Thomas–Kilmann `5` Styles**, *Figure 8.1b*):
   - **Competing** (*High Assertive, Low Cooperative*): Win–lose dominance (*vital in emergencies or unpopular cost cuts; risks resentment*).
   - **Collaborating** (*High Assertive, High Cooperative*): Win–win integrative problem-solving (*best when both parties' concerns are too vital to compromise and trust/time exist*).
   - **Avoiding** (*Low Assertive, Low Cooperative*): Withdrawing/suppressing (*suits trivial issues or cooling off; leaves root problems festering*).
   - **Accommodating** (*Low Assertive, High Cooperative*): Self-sacrifice to preserve harmony (*smart when you are wrong or building goodwill; risks exploitation*).
   - **Compromising** (*Moderate Assertive, Moderate Cooperative*): Splitting the difference (`50–50`) under time pressure (*fast temporary settlement, leaves potential value uncreated — e.g., **Alex `40%` group grade** dilemma!*).
4. **Stage IV — Behavior**: Overt statements, actions, escalation/de-escalation techniques.
5. **Stage V — Outcomes**: Either **Functional** (better decisions, creativity, self-evaluation) or **Dysfunctional** (gridlock, destroyed cohesion, dissolution).

### 14.3 Power Bases (`French & Raven`), Dependence Postulate (`Maya`), and `9` Influence Tactics
Unlike **Leadership** (requires goal compatibility and mostly downward influence), **Power** is the **capacity $A$ has to influence $B$'s behavior so $B$ acts in accordance with $A$'s wishes** — requiring **NO shared goals**, only **Dependence** (*The Devil Wears Prada: Miranda Priestly vs. Andy*)!

1. **Five Bases of Power (`French & Raven`)**:
   - **Formal Power** *(derived from organizational position)*:
     - **Coercive**: Fear of negative results (*firing, demotion, cold shoulder*).
     - **Reward**: Control over valued outcomes (*pay, bonuses, promotions, prized schedules*).
     - **Legitimate**: Formal structural authority to issue orders within scope (*Miranda Priestly*).
   - **Personal Power** *(resides in the individual regardless of formal title — **Strongest positive predictor of employee satisfaction, commitment & performance!**)*:
     - **Expert**: Influence based on **special skills, rare knowledge, or technical mastery**.
     - **Referent**: Influence based on **admiration, charisma, personal respect, or wanting to be like that person**.

2. **The General Postulate of Dependence** *(Core Mechanism of Power!)*:
   > **$B$'s dependence on $A$ is maximized when the resource $A$ controls exhibits all three:**
   > $$\text{Power of } A \propto \text{Importance} \times \text{Scarcity} \times \text{Non-Substitutability}$$
   - **Lesson 14 *Maya* Case (`Sole Backend Engineer`)**: When Maya holds critical deployment knowledge nobody else knows (`High Importance + High Scarcity + Low Substitutability`), she wields huge informal dependence power (*conversely, Andy with `3` outside job offers slashes Miranda's power by raising her own **BATNA***!). **Three management remedies to reduce single-point dependence risk**: *(1) Cross-train peers*, *(2) Document institutional knowledge*, *(3) Retain & engage strategically*.

3. **Nine Influence Tactics (`R&J Ch. 13` & `Lesson 14`)**:
   *(Tested via the **Flexible Hours Pitch** exercise: `Option A = Rational persuasion [data/efficiency]`, `Option B = Inspirational appeal [values/purpose]`, `Option C = Consultation [inviting co-design]`)*
   - **Most Effective Across Directions (Upward, Downward & Lateral)**:
     1. **Rational Persuasion** *(facts, data & logical arguments — **ONLY tactic consistently effective upward!**)*
     2. **Inspirational Appeals** *(linking to shared values/aspirations)*
     3. **Consultation** *(involving target in planning how to implement)*
   - **Conditional / Moderate Tactics**:
     4. **Ingratiation** *(flattery/friendliness before asking)*
     5. **Personal Appeals** *(asking based on friendship/loyalty — lateral best)*
     6. **Exchange** *(trading favors/benefits)*
     7. **Coalition Tactics** *(enlisting allies to pressure target)*
   - **Least Effective / Risky Backfire**:
     8. **Legitimating Tactics** *(citing authority/rules)*
     9. **Pressure** *(warnings, repeated demands, threats — triggers resistance!)*

   *(Effectiveness hinges on **three moderators**: **Audience** [upward vs. downward], **Political Skill & Credibility**, and **Organizational/Cultural Context**.)*

### 14.4 Organizational Politics, Voice vs. Silence
Because organizations allocate **scarce resources** under **ambiguous criteria**, **Organizational Politics** (*activities not required as part of formal roles that attempt to influence advantage distribution — illustrated by the **Succession Boardroom Vote**!*) inevitably arise. High perceived unfair politics drive **anxiety, lower job satisfaction, defensive behaviors (*buck-passing, stalling, goldbricking*), and turnover**. In politically charged climates, employees choose carefully between **Voice** (speaking up constructively) vs. **Defensive Silence** (withholding ideas/risks out of fear — looping right back to *Lesson 4 Psychological Safety & Lesson 6 Awestruck deference!*).

### 14.5 Distributive vs. Integrative Bargaining, `BATNA` & `5` Negotiation Steps
**Negotiation** is a process in which two or more parties exchange goods or services and attempt to agree on the exchange rate (*illustrated by **Spotify vs. Artist**: `€200k vs €500k` cash advance, exclusivity window, playlist promotion*). Two core strategies govern outcomes:

| Criterion | Distributive Bargaining *(Claiming Value)* | Integrative Bargaining *(Creating Value)* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Goal** | Get as much of a **fixed pie** as possible | **Expand the pie** so *both* parties win |
| **Motivation** | **Win–Lose** (zero-sum) | **Win–Win** (trade across **unequally weighted issues**) |
| **Info Sharing** | **Low** (hide true reservation price!) | **High** (reveal underlying interests/priorities) |
| **Relationship Focus** | **Short-term** | **Long-term ongoing partnership** |
| **Spotify vs. Artist** | Fighting purely over `€200k` vs `€500k` cash fee | Lower advance (`€250k`) + **high editorial playlist push + `12-mo` short exclusivity**! |

- **Bargaining Zone (`Distributive`)**: Each side holds an aspirational **Target Point** and a walk-away **Resistance Point**. Only when Buyer's resistance $\ge$ Seller's resistance does a **Positive Bargaining Zone** exist!
- **BATNA (*Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement*)**: The lowest-value deal you can safely accept, because if talks collapse you walk directly to your **BATNA**. Knowing (and strengthening!) your BATNA — like Andy holding competing job offers — anchors leverage and prevents bad deals.
- **Five Steps of the Negotiation Process (`R&J Exhibit 14-6` & `Lesson 14 Slide 34`)**:
  1. **Preparation and Planning** *(define goals, assess opponent's goals, establish **your BATNA**!)*
  2. **Definition of Ground Rules** *(who negotiates, where, timeline, issues covered)*
  3. **Clarification and Justification** *(explain, amplify, bolster opening demands with evidence)*
  4. **Bargaining and Problem Solving** *(give-and-take concessions & integrative creative packages)*
  5. **Closure and Implementation** *(formalizing agreement & monitoring follow-through)*

**Final Course Synthesis (`One Situation, Three Lenses`, *Lesson 14 Slides 35–37*)**: Every dramatic organizational breakdown — **Twitter/Musk** (Conflict type escalation + Coercive power), **Miranda Priestly** (Legitimate/Coercive power + high-anxiety silence), and **Logan Roy / Succession** (high-stakes Coalition Politics + Zero-sum Bargaining) — looks shallow through a single chapter and **crystal clear** when viewed simultaneously through **Conflict + Power + Politics**!

### 15.2 Five-Step MCQ Distractor Elimination Protocol
Before picking `A–E` on any EXC 3460 vignette, execute these five fast checks:
1. **Check the OB Level (`Micro vs. Meso vs. Macro`)**: Is the question asking about *individual* perception/motivation, *group* team norms/leadership, or *organizational* culture/structure? Eliminate options from the wrong analytical level immediately.
2. **Check the Valence / Direction (`Constructive vs. Destructive`, `Active vs. Passive`, `Internal vs. External`)**: In *EVLN*, *Einarsen*, *Conflict types*, *Herzberg*, and *Kelley*, direction alone usually eliminates `2` to `3` options cleanly!
3. **Verify Static vs. Adaptable Assumption**: Remember Fiedler (`LPC` style **fixed**; change situation) vs. Hersey–Blanchard (leader **adapts** `R1–R4` style); Maslow (needs active now) vs. Vroom (multiplicative **expectation**); Rational (**Maximize**) vs. Bounded (**Satisfice**).
4. **Spot the Look-Alike Twin**: Most wrong answers on BI's `A–E` stems are **real OB concepts from the *same* chapter** (*e.g., Groupshift next to Groupthink; Job Enlargement next to Job Enrichment; Cooptation next to Participation; Invisible Cage next to Autonomy Paradox*). Apply the **exact contrast matrix** in **[Worked Examples](obsidian://open?vault=Obsidian%20Vault&file=EXC3460-Obsidian/EXC3460-support/Worked%20Examples)**!
5. **Reject Universal "Always / Never" Absolutes**: Because OB is a contingency discipline (`Behavior = f(Person, Situation)`), options claiming *"always motivates regardless of context"* or *"always beats organic structure"* are nearly always false distractors unless quoting an explicit definition (*e.g., Relationship conflict is almost always dysfunctional*).
